Your skepticism is half right. The pool theory has the correct shape but may have the wrong noun in it. A hang that lands on a different test every time, only under CI, almost always means some resource shared across tests is being leaked or contended, and the test that hangs is the victim rather than the cause: it is simply the next one to ask for the thing that ran out. Before going further, check whether your runner randomizes test order per run. If it does, "always a different test" is exactly what a single deterministic culprit would look like, and the observation carries much less information than it seems to.

Connections are one candidate resource among several that fit equally well. A pool with no checkout timeout will block forever once every connection is held by a leaked transaction, which is the classic version. But a thread or executor pool sized from CPU count deadlocks the same way when a task submitted to the pool blocks waiting on another task in the same pool; your laptop has enough cores to hide it and a CI container capped at one or two does not. A socket with no read timeout will hang indefinitely when the CI network path silently drops an idle connection, and NAT conntrack tables commonly evict at five or fifteen minutes, so watch for hangs that begin after a suspiciously round idle interval. If any integration test spawns a subprocess, a full pipe buffer will deadlock parent and child against each other, and CI often turns log verbosity up far enough to cross the 64KB threshold that local runs never reach. Parallel workers sharing one database schema can also block on row or advisory locks in a way a serial local run never produces.

The way to tell these apart is to stop reasoning from priors and get a stack dump out of the hung process. Set a job timeout below whatever your CI platform enforces, and have that timeout trigger a dump of every thread in every relevant process rather than a bare kill: `py-spy dump --pid` for Python, `jstack` for the JVM, SIGQUIT for Go, `--report-on-signal` or `why-is-node-running` for Node. Capture `ss -tanp` and the database's own view at the same moment, meaning `pg_stat_activity` with `state` and `wait_event` for Postgres or `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` for MySQL. The hypotheses separate cleanly in that output. Pool exhaustion shows every worker parked in an acquire call, with the database side reporting connections idle in transaction. Executor starvation shows workers blocked on a future that only a queued task could complete. A lock fight shows `wait_event_type` of Lock and a visible blocker. A pipe deadlock shows the child in write and the parent in waitpid. A dead socket shows a thread in recv against a connection the peer has long since forgotten.

Two cheap changes are worth making regardless of which one it turns out to be. Put a finite timeout on every blocking operation, especially pool checkout and socket reads, so the failure surfaces as an error with a stack instead of silence. And log the test that finished immediately before the hang along with the random seed, because with a leaked resource the informative name is the leaker's, not the victim's. If one particular predecessor keeps showing up across incidents, you have your answer without needing the dump at all.

To reproduce it locally, match the CI constraints rather than the CI script: same image, same worker count, `--cpus=1 --memory=2g`, same log level, then loop the suite a hundred times. If forcing the suite to run serially makes the hang go away entirely, the cause is cross-test interference and you can stop considering everything else.

Your skepticism is half right. Connection pool exhaustion is a plausible member of the right family, but the family is larger than that one member, and "always a different test" is the clue that tells you which family you're in rather than which member.

A test that hangs in its own logic hangs at the same place every time. Yours doesn't, so either something accumulates across the run and tips over at whatever test happens to be executing when the threshold is crossed, or something in the environment lands at an arbitrary point in wall-clock time. A leaked connection is the first kind: the test that hangs is simply the one that asked for connection N+1, and its identity is an accident. But a leaked semaphore permit, a fixed-size thread pool where a queued task waits on another task in the same pool, or an unclosed transaction all produce the same signature. So does the second kind, for entirely different reasons.

The candidates I'd actually weigh, given that it reproduces only in CI:

Shared-database lock contention is the one I'd suspect first if your integration tests run in parallel workers against a single database. Postgres will break a true deadlock, but it will not break a plain lock wait; a `SELECT FOR UPDATE` sitting behind a session that's idle in transaction waits forever unless you've set `lock_timeout`. Locally you probably run serially, so the contention never arises. Test-order randomisation makes this look non-deterministic even when it's a deterministic interaction between one pair of tests.

Missing socket timeouts are next. On your laptop the dependency is on loopback and either answers or refuses immediately. In CI a container can be scheduled, DNS-resolvable, and still black-hole your SYN or accept the connection without ever serving it. With no connect or read timeout configured, that's an unbounded block, and the randomness comes from container startup ordering rather than from your code.

Parallelism and sizing differences deserve attention because they explain "never locally" without requiring any behavioural difference at all. Many pool libraries size themselves from CPU count, so a pool that's comfortably large on your ten-core machine is starved on a two-vCPU runner, and the same leak that is invisible locally becomes fatal in CI at one run in twenty.

The dark horse is output backpressure. If the job captures stdout through a pipe that nothing is draining, a process writing verbose logs blocks on `write` once the buffer fills, and that presents exactly as a hang at an arbitrary test.

To tell these apart, stop letting the platform kill the job and make the hang produce an artifact instead. Set a per-test timeout well below the job timeout, and on expiry dump every thread's stack: `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later` in Python or `py-spy dump`, `jstack` or `SIGQUIT` on the JVM, `SIGQUIT` for Go, active handles for Node. One such dump usually collapses this entire list to a single candidate, because a parked thread names its own reason for parking. Alongside it, capture:

- `pg_stat_activity` with `state`, `wait_event_type`, `wait_event` and `query_start`, plus `pg_locks`, so a lock wait or an idle-in-transaction session identifies itself
- your pool's in-use, idle and waiting counts, logged after every test, since a monotonic climb across the run is the leak signature and confirms or kills the pool theory in one run
- the random seed and the resulting test order, printed unconditionally
- worker count, `nproc`, and the pool's configured maximum

The predictions then separate cleanly. If it's a leak, the ordinal position of the hang stays roughly constant while the test name varies, and the pool counts climb. If it's an order-dependent interaction, replaying the recorded seed reproduces it, which also gives you a fast bisect. If it's infrastructure, the hang correlates with a slow dependency rather than with anything in the suite. And if serial single-worker runs in CI never hang while parallel ones do, everything network-related drops away and you're looking at shared state or contention.

The seed logging and the stack dump on timeout are worth doing before any further theorising; one in twenty means roughly two or three runs to catch it, and you'd rather spend those runs collecting evidence than confirming a guess. Happy to look at the CI config and the fixture setup if you want to point me at them.

The detail worth building on is that it lands on a different test each time. A test that hangs at itself is a test with a bug; a hang that wanders is nearly always something shared, so whichever test happens to be running when the shared thing goes bad is the one that gets blamed. Pool exhaustion fits that shape, which is presumably why it was suggested, but so do about four other families, and they're distinguishable if you set things up to capture evidence rather than argue from plausibility.

The first family is accumulation across the run. Something leaks a little per test until a threshold is crossed, and the crossing point drifts because tests vary in how much they leak and in what order the runner interleaves them. Connections are one candidate; file descriptors, unreaped threads, ephemeral ports stuck in TIME_WAIT, and transactions left open holding row locks are all equally good ones, and the last of these often looks exactly like pool exhaustion from the client side. The signature of this whole family is that the hang correlates with position in the run rather than with test identity: if you shuffle the order with different seeds and the hang keeps landing around the same ordinal, you're accumulating something.

The second family is the shape of the CI machine. Runners typically have two or four cores where your laptop has ten or more, and any pool sized from the CPU count shrinks accordingly. A test that occupies a worker while awaiting a task queued behind it on the same executor deadlocks reliably at two cores and never at ten. Latency differences do similar damage to condition-variable and callback code: a response that arrives locally after you've started waiting arrives on CI before, and the wakeup is lost. These reproduce locally the moment you stop running under laptop conditions, which is the single highest-value experiment here.

The third family is peculiar to running without a terminal, and it gets overlooked because nobody thinks of it as a concurrency bug at all. A subprocess whose output nobody drains blocks once it fills the pipe buffer, at about 64 KB, and sits there forever; the amount a test logs varies, so which test trips it varies. Similarly, anything that reads stdin under CI, whether a credential prompt, a confirmation, or a stray debugger, blocks on a descriptor that will never produce a byte or an EOF.

The fourth family isn't really a hang: it's a missing timeout turning an ordinary failure into an infinite wait. If your HTTP and database clients have no socket timeout, then a dependency container that OOMs, restarts, or loses a DNS lookup produces a thread parked in read forever. Worth checking alongside this is contention between concurrent CI jobs, since one shared database, schema, or advisory lock across two overlapping runs produces exactly the sort of one-in-twenty rate you're describing, and locally you never have a second run competing with you.

To tell these apart, make the hang produce a stack trace instead of a timeout message. Wrap the test step so that at, say, 80% of the job's time limit a watchdog dumps every thread's stack and then kills the process: SIGQUIT for a JVM, `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later` or `py-spy dump` for Python, SIGQUIT for Go's goroutine dump, `SIGUSR1` plus the inspector for Node. In the same hook, capture `ss -tanp`, the open file descriptors of the test process, `pg_stat_activity` or its equivalent from the database, the dependency containers' logs, and `/proc/pressure/*`. Add per-test timeouts and a timestamped line at each test's start and end so you know precisely which test was in flight. One capture settles the question that no amount of discussion will.

Reading the capture is then mostly mechanical. Many threads parked in `getConnection` or `acquire` with the pool reporting all connections in use, held by call sites belonging to already-finished tests, is genuine pool exhaustion. A single thread in a socket read with no matching connection in `ss` output is the missing-timeout case, and the container logs at that timestamp will tell you what died. Every worker waiting on a future whose task is still sitting in the same executor's queue is starvation from core count. A child process blocked in `write` on fd 1 is the pipe case, and anything sitting in `read` on fd 0 is the stdin case. Nothing blocked at all, with the process burning CPU, points instead at a retry loop or a livelock.

Alongside that, work on making it happen more often, because a one-in-twenty rate is unusable for iteration. Run the suite locally under CI conditions: `--cpus=2 --memory=2g` under Docker, output redirected to a file rather than a terminal, no tty, and the same container images the pipeline uses, then loop it thirty times overnight. Sweep the order seed while you're at it. Meanwhile the pool hypothesis is cheap to falsify directly, so it's worth doing even though I'd rank it below the core-count and missing-timeout explanations: emit the pool's active and idle gauges after every test. If active never climbs toward the maximum across the run, the theory is dead and you've spent twenty minutes; if it ratchets upward and never comes back down, you've found your leak and the stack dump will tell you which test opened it.

I'd keep it in Postgres, with one piece of precision that matters more than the same-versus-separate framing: the same *database* as application data, in its own schema, declaratively partitioned by month from day one. A separate Postgres database on the same cluster would give you most of the operational downsides and none of the join benefit, since you'd be back to FDW or dblink to reach user records.

The join requirement is what decides it. Support investigations are a daily-cadence need, and "join audit events against user records" is a one-line query when both live in the same database and a small integration project when they don't. The usual answer from the separate-store camp is to denormalise user attributes into each event, but attributes drift, and the support question is often about the user as they are now rather than as they were captured. Once you're reconstructing joins in application code across two systems, the cost lands on every investigation, not just the unusual ones.

There's a second argument for co-location that tends to go unmentioned in these debates: writing the audit event inside the same transaction as the action it records gives you atomicity for free. The event and the change it describes either both commit or neither does. Any pipeline that ships events to a separate store, whether through Kafka, a queue, or a batched writer, introduces a window where the two can disagree, and reconciling that window is exactly the work you don't want to be doing when an auditor asks why the log shows a change the data doesn't.

The separate-store camp is right about one thing, and it isn't volume. Two million events a day is about twenty-five writes per second on average, which Postgres does without noticing. What they're right about is that "append-only" needs to be enforced rather than assumed. You can get most of the way there inside Postgres: put the audit schema under a role that the application connects as with INSERT and SELECT only, revoke UPDATE and DELETE from every role the app touches, and add a hash chain over each row so that any retroactive edit breaks the chain from that point forward. Periodically anchoring the chain head somewhere outside the database gives you tamper-evidence that a database superuser can't quietly undo.

What actually threatens the co-located design is not write throughput but the size of the corpus. Seven years at this rate is roughly five billion rows, somewhere between two and five terabytes depending on payload size, and that lands on your backup window, your restore time, and your failover story for the application. Restoring the app after an incident should not mean restoring seven years of audit history first. Partitioning by month is what makes this tractable, both because it lets you back up and detach old partitions independently and because it's the only way you'll survive a schema change later. Retrofitting partitioning onto a two-billion-row table is a project; declaring it at table creation costs an afternoon. If you go this route, the partitioning decision has to happen before the table does.

That gives you a natural tiering: keep a hot window live, perhaps twelve to eighteen months, which covers essentially every support investigation, and export detached partitions as Parquet to object storage with Object Lock enabled for the seven-year tail. Queries against the old tail get slower and more deliberate, which is an accurate reflection of how often you'll run them.

The thing that would change my recommendation is a compliance regime that names the storage medium rather than the outcome. If your auditors work from something like SEC 17a-4, where non-rewritable, non-erasable media is a stated requirement rather than a property you demonstrate, then the hash-chain approach won't satisfy them and you should ship to a purpose-built store and accept the join pain. Worth finding out which kind of requirement you're under before the team spends more time split, because it's the only input here that flips the answer.

I'd keep it in Postgres, but not in the same schema as application data, and not for all seven years. Start with the numbers, because they decide more here than the philosophy does. Two million events a day is about twenty-three writes a second on average and maybe a few hundred at peak, which is nothing for an instance already serving application traffic. The problem isn't the write rate, it's the accumulation: seven years is roughly five billion rows, somewhere between two and five terabytes with indexes depending on payload size. That volume stays perfectly queryable in Postgres if it's partitioned, but it changes the cost of every operation you perform on the cluster as a whole. Base backups get slower, your restore time objective gets worse, major version upgrades get harder to schedule, and all of that is being paid on behalf of data you read a handful of times a year, so the tax lands on the application rather than on the audit log that incurred it.

The join requirement is weaker than it looks. If an investigation needs to join audit events to user records to find out who did something, that implies the audit rows store a user id and little else, which is a correctness problem independent of where you put them. Joining a three-year-old event to the current users table tells you the actor's name, role and team as of today, not as of the event. An audit record should be a self-describing snapshot: actor identity, display name, role, tenant, all captured at write time. Once you denormalise that way, most investigations stop needing the join, and the ones that remain are usually "show me everything this person did", which is a filter on a denormalised column.

Concretely, then: same database, separate schema, monthly partitions, and a dedicated role holding INSERT and SELECT and nothing else. Keep a hot window attached, ninety days or a year depending on how far back support actually reaches, which is a couple hundred million rows at most and where joins against user records work normally on the rare occasion you want one. Detach older partitions on a schedule and write them to object storage as Parquet, where they cost almost nothing and stay queryable with Athena or DuckDB when compliance asks. You get joins where joins are useful and the seven-year tail stays out of your backup path.

One caveat on "append-only", since the phrase is carrying a lot of weight in this debate. A Postgres table whose writing role only has INSERT satisfies most auditors, but it isn't WORM: a superuser, or anyone with filesystem access, can rewrite history without leaving evidence. If your compliance regime genuinely requires immutability rather than an immutability policy, no Postgres configuration gets you there, and you want S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the archived partitions. It's worth reading what the regime actually says before the team argues further, because the two readings point to different designs. Independently of that, a hash chain, each row carrying a hash of the previous row's contents, gives you tamper evidence for one column's cost and survives the move to object storage.

The case for shipping everything to a separate store from day one is real, but it's mostly about organisational boundaries rather than technical ones: it's much easier to argue the audit log can't be tampered with when the application holds no credentials that could tamper with it. If your auditors or your customers are actually asking that question, pay the cost and take the cross-store stitching as the price. If nobody is asking it, splitting by age gives you the same properties on the data that matters while investigations stay a single query.

I'd keep it in Postgres, but not in the same schema as application data: give the audit log its own schema with its own writer role, partitioned by month, in the same cluster you already run. The reason is that at your volume the arguments for a separate store are weaker than they sound, while the cost of running a second storage technology is real and permanent, and starting in Postgres keeps the separation cheap to do later if you need it.

Start with the numbers, because they set the ceiling on the whole discussion. Two million events a day is about twenty-three writes per second averaged out, so call it a few hundred per second at peak. Postgres will not notice that alongside your application traffic. Seven years at that rate is roughly five billion rows, which at a realistic 500 bytes to 1 KB per event lands somewhere between 2.5 and 5 TB before indexes. The volume is not a throughput problem; it is a storage and operations problem, and it shows up in backup duration, restore time, and what you're paying for primary-tier storage to hold data nobody has read in four years. Monthly partitions address most of that: you can put older partitions on a cheaper tablespace, and the seven-year expiry becomes a DROP TABLE instead of a delete that runs for a week and bloats everything it touches.

The join requirement is the argument most often used to settle this, and I think it deserves less weight than your team is probably giving it. Support investigations are interactive, scoped to one user and usually a narrow window, and they return hundreds of rows rather than millions. More importantly, an audit event should record who the actor was at the time it happened, not carry a foreign key that resolves to whoever that account belongs to today. If someone's email changed, or their role was revoked, or the account was merged into another, a live join actively misrepresents the history you're keeping the log to preserve. Denormalising actor identity into the event at write time is better audit design on its own merits, and it happens to remove most of the pressure to keep the two datasets joinable.

What a separate append-only store genuinely buys you is the guarantee that the application cannot rewrite its own history, and you should check whether your auditor requires that specific property or merely requires that you can demonstrate it. In Postgres you get most of the way there by having the application write through a role with INSERT granted and UPDATE and DELETE revoked, with schema ownership held elsewhere. If the requirement is stronger, a hash chain over each event, sealed periodically to external storage, gives you tamper evidence without moving the data. Neither of these is exotic, and both are considerably less work than operating a second system with its own backup story, access controls, monitoring, and on-call knowledge.

The condition that should change my answer is scale. If volume grows an order of magnitude, or if restoring the application database in an incident starts being gated by audit data you'd never need in the first hour, split it out. Because you'd be splitting Postgres to Postgres, that migration is a logical dump of one schema rather than a rewrite of every write path, and the recent partitions that support actually queries can stay where they are while the cold ones move. Building the cheap option first is what preserves that.

I haven't found the cause, but the shape of the failure narrows it usefully, so here is what the evidence does and doesn't support. The short runs aren't random: in the last eight, the low ones fall on 23, 26 and 29 August, three days apart, and they cluster tightly near 23k rows against roughly 48k for the others. Their duration halves too, about seven minutes against fifteen, and that is the detail I'd lean on: the job isn't doing the full amount of work and discarding half of it; it is finding half as much work to do. So the problem is more likely upstream of the write loop, in `fetch_events` or the window it's handed, than in the transaction in `run()` at `jobs/nightly_rollup.py:23` where I'd otherwise have started.

I couldn't get past that because two things I'd need are still unchecked. I read `run()` and the two lines of `jobs/scheduler.py:61` that build the window, but not `fetch_events` itself, so I don't know whether it pages, whether it caps, or what it does when a page fails partway. Commit 9d02e1c, "retry transient fetch errors", looks relevant in that light, since a retry wrapper that exhausts its attempts and returns what it has collected so far would produce exactly this signature: a run that is short, fast, and still reports `ok`. I'm guessing at its contents, though, and it may do nothing of the kind. The three-day spacing is also thin evidence, resting on eight of the thirty recorded runs.

`tug` pushes a local directory to an S3-compatible bucket. It is one-way by design: the local tree is the source of truth, and nothing on the remote is ever copied back down. On each run it compares each local file against the size and modification time of the corresponding remote object and uploads only what differs, so a second push over an unchanged tree costs little beyond the bucket listing.

## Installation

With a Go toolchain:

```
go install github.com/you/tug@latest
```

Or download a prebuilt binary for your platform from the releases page, make it executable, and put it somewhere on your `PATH`:

```
curl -Lo tug https://github.com/you/tug/releases/latest/download/tug-linux-amd64
chmod +x tug && sudo mv tug /usr/local/bin/
```

`tug` looks for `~/.tug/credentials` first. The file is a simple key/value list, and it should not be world-readable:

```

secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
endpoint = https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
region = us-east-1
```

If that file is missing, `tug` falls back to the environment: `TUG_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `TUG_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `TUG_ENDPOINT` and `TUG_REGION`. Environment variables are the better fit for CI, where writing a credentials file to disk buys you nothing.

## Usage

Every command takes a local directory and a bucket destination, and every command accepts `--dry-run`, which prints the work that would be done and exits without touching the remote. Getting into the habit of a dry run first is worth the extra keystrokes, since a mistyped source path is otherwise indistinguishable from a large legitimate upload until it is finished.

```
tug push   ./site  s3://my-bucket/prefix
tug status ./site  s3://my-bucket/prefix
tug verify ./site  s3://my-bucket/prefix
```

`tug push` uploads every local file whose size or mtime differs from the remote object, and every file that has no remote object at all. Files that match on both attributes are skipped without being read.

`tug status` performs the same comparison and reports what a push would do, but never uploads. It is the read-only sibling of `push --dry-run` and is safe to wire into a prompt or a monitoring check.

`tug verify` ignores mtimes and compares checksums instead, which catches the cases mtime comparison cannot: a file whose contents changed while its size and timestamp were preserved, or an upload that was truncated or corrupted in transit. Use it after a migration or when you have reason to distrust a previous push, rather than on every run.

## Ignoring files

If a `.tugignore` file is present at the root of the local directory, `tug` reads it using gitignore syntax, including negation with `!` and directory-only patterns with a trailing slash:

```

node_modules/
.DS_Store
!important.log
```

Ignored paths are excluded from all three commands, so a file you ignore will not be uploaded by `push`, will not appear in `status`, and will not be checked by `verify`.

There is no delete propagation. Removing a file locally leaves the remote object in place, and the only way to clear it is to delete it yourself through your provider's console or CLI. Anything using `tug` as a mirror rather than an append-only push should account for that.

Files larger than 5GB will fail, because `tug` does not yet implement multipart upload and a single PUT is capped at that size by the S3 API. The error is reported per file and does not abort the rest of the run.

`verify` is slow on large buckets. It fetches the ETag of every object rather than working from a listing, which means one request per file and a runtime that scales linearly with object count. On a bucket of any real size, expect to run it deliberately rather than on a schedule.

```

```

region = us-east-1

export TUG_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export TUG_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export TUG_ENDPOINT=https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com
export TUG_REGION=nyc3
```

Environment variables take precedence over the credentials file. If neither source supplies a key, `tug` exits without contacting the network rather than falling back to anonymous access.

`tug push <dir> <bucket>[/prefix]` walks the local directory and uploads everything that differs from the remote. Passing `--dry-run` prints the same report of what would be uploaded, skipped and totalled, but performs no writes; it is worth running the first time you point `tug` at an unfamiliar bucket.

tug push ./public assets.example.com/site --dry-run
```

`tug status <dir> <bucket>[/prefix]` compares the two sides and reports the difference without uploading anything. It is the read-only sibling of `push --dry-run` and is the right command for a health check or a pre-commit hook, since it never opens a file for reading beyond its metadata.

Rather than trusting size and mtime, it computes a checksum for each local file and compares it against the remote object's ETag, which will catch a truncated upload or a file that was modified in place without its timestamp changing. Because the timestamp heuristic that makes `push` fast is exactly what `verify` refuses to rely on, this command is much slower; run it after an interrupted push or on a schedule, not on every deploy.

```

.DS_Store
!important.log
```

Ignored files are never uploaded and are not treated as remote-only leftovers, so adding a pattern after a push leaves the already-uploaded objects in place.

There is no delete propagation. Removing a file locally does not remove the corresponding object from the bucket, and `tug` will not report it as a difference. If you need the remote to be an exact mirror, you will have to prune it yourself.

`verify` scales poorly. It issues a request per object to fetch each ETag, so on a bucket with hundreds of thousands of keys the command can take hours and will generate a corresponding number of billable API calls. Scope it to a prefix when you can.

RQ is considerably simpler than Celery and would have been a smaller thing to learn, but it still requires Redis, so it does not relieve the operational objection, and it still cannot commit a job atomically with the database write that produced it. Choosing it would mean accepting the main cost of the broker approach while getting less than Celery offers in return.

# Use Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` for background job queueing

## Status

Accepted. Implemented in Q3.

## Context

We are replacing the background job runner we wrote in-house. It has served us to this point, but it lacks durable retries, scheduling, and any visibility into in-flight work, and we do not want to keep extending it. We evaluated three replacements: Celery backed by Redis, RQ backed by Redis, and a queue built on Postgres using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.

Four properties of our situation drove the comparison. The first is volume. We process roughly 30,000 jobs a day and peak around 40 per second, which is one to two orders of magnitude below the load a dedicated broker is designed to absorb. Throughput was therefore not a deciding factor; we are choosing among options that all comfortably clear the bar we actually need to clear.

The second is atomicity, and it turned out to be the decisive one. A large share of our jobs are enqueued inside a database transaction that also writes application state, and the two must succeed or fail together. A job that fires against state its transaction rolled back is a bug, and a committed transaction whose job never arrives is a different bug. A broker running in its own process cannot join a Postgres transaction, so obtaining this property with Celery or RQ means building a transactional outbox: insert the job into a Postgres table inside the caller's transaction, then run a relay process that reads committed rows and publishes them to Redis. The outbox is itself a Postgres queue, and adopting it would leave us operating a Postgres queue *and* a Redis broker to get a guarantee the Postgres queue already provides on its own.

The third is operational surface. We run Postgres today with backups, monitoring, failover, and an on-call rotation that knows how it behaves under stress. Redis would be a second stateful service to provision, patch, monitor, size for memory, and page someone about at three in the morning, and its durability model would need its own decisions about persistence and failover before we could rely on it for work we cannot afford to drop.

The fourth is team experience. Nobody on the team has run Celery in production. Celery's power lives in a wide configuration surface, and so do its failure modes: prefetch counts, `acks_late`, visibility timeouts, result backends, and worker pool types are all places where a misconfiguration produces duplicated or silently lost work under conditions that only appear during an incident. Learning that surface well enough to operate it confidently is a real cost, paid at a time when the queue is new and least understood. RQ is far smaller and would have been much cheaper to learn, but it does not address the atomicity requirement, which left it needing the same outbox as Celery with fewer features in return.

## Decision

We will use Postgres as the queue. Jobs are rows in a `jobs` table; enqueueing is an `INSERT` in the caller's transaction, so a job becomes visible exactly when the writes that justify it commit. Workers claim batches with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, which lets concurrent workers pull disjoint sets of rows without blocking one another or serialising on a single hot lock. We are writing our own retry, backoff, and scheduling logic on top of that primitive rather than adopting a framework.

## Consequences

We accept a throughput ceiling in the low hundreds of jobs per second. Beyond that, polling and row contention make Postgres queueing an unhappy fit, and we would need to move to a purpose-built broker. At 40 per second peak we have roughly an order of magnitude of headroom, which is enough that growth would give us warning rather than an outage, but the ceiling is real and we should treat sustained load above about 150 per second as the signal to revisit this record.

We take on roughly 400 lines of retry, backoff, and scheduling code that Celery would have supplied. This is code we must test, document, and maintain, and it is the part of the system most likely to harbour subtle bugs around clock handling and repeated delivery. The compensating benefit is that the logic is ours, written against our semantics, debuggable with the same tools and the same SQL we use for everything else, and inspectable by anyone on the team without learning a framework first.

Long-running jobs hold a connection from the pool for their duration, which couples job design to database capacity in a way a Redis-backed worker would not. We size the worker pool separately from the web pool so that a backlog of slow jobs cannot starve request handling, and jobs that are expected to run for minutes should be structured to release their claim and checkpoint rather than hold a connection open across the whole run.

Against those costs, we add no new service to the on-call surface, we get exactly-once enqueueing without an outbox, and the queue is queryable: the state of pending, running, and failed work is available to anyone who can write a `SELECT`, with no separate introspection tooling to build or learn.

# Incident postmortem: image upload failure following media-service v4.7.0

Image uploads failed for every user for 2 hours and 36 minutes on 14 July 2025, from 09:12 to 11:48 UTC. Roughly 18,000 upload attempts failed during the window. No data was lost: uploads that failed were rejected outright rather than partially written, and the retry backlog drained cleanly once the service recovered. The cause was a deploy of `media-service` v4.7.0, whose new thumbnail generator invoked an `ImageMagick` binary that is not present in the production container image. The failure was total and immediate, but it was invisible to our alerting for 49 minutes and unattended for 51, because the service reported its failures with an HTTP 200 and an error body while our alert watched the 5xx rate.

## Timeline (UTC)

- 09:12 — `media-service` v4.7.0 deploys to production.
- 09:14 — Upload error rate rises from 0.2% to 100%. No alert fires.
- 09:41 — First customer support ticket arrives.
- 10:03 — An engineer notices the ticket volume and begins investigating.
- 10:20 — Cause identified: v4.7.0 requires an `ImageMagick` binary absent from the production image.
- 10:31 — Rollback to the previous version begins.
- 10:44 — Rollback completes; uploads recover.
- 11:48 — Backlog of retried uploads drains; incident closed.

## What happened

Version 4.7.0 rewrote thumbnail generation to shell out to `ImageMagick` rather than use the previous in-process library. That dependency was added to the Dockerfile used by CI but not to the one used to build the production image, so the binary was simply missing at runtime. Every upload reached the thumbnail step, failed to execute the binary, and returned an error to the client. Because the failure was in a required step of the upload path, there was no partial success: the feature was either working or entirely broken, and after 09:14 it was entirely broken.

Two safeguards that should have caught this before production did not. The integration test suite mocks the thumbnail generator, so the tests exercised the calling code without ever executing the binary and passed against an image that could not have run it. CI also builds from a different Dockerfile than production does, so the artifact that passed the pipeline was not the artifact that shipped. Together these meant the deploy carried no signal that anything was wrong.

## Why nobody was paged

The upload endpoint returned HTTP 200 with an application-level error in the response body. Our alert was defined on the 5xx rate, which stayed flat at its normal baseline throughout the incident, so the monitoring system's view of the service was that it remained perfectly healthy while it served zero successful uploads. Detection therefore fell to customers, who filed the first ticket 27 minutes into the outage, and to an engineer who happened to notice the ticket volume 22 minutes after that. Once someone was actually looking, diagnosis took 17 minutes and remediation another 24, which is roughly what we would expect; the loss was almost entirely in the 51 minutes before anyone knew.

## Action items

The alert is the highest-priority fix, since it is what turned a fast-to-diagnose bug into a two-and-a-half-hour outage. We should alert on the application-level upload success rate rather than on HTTP status, and separately treat the 200-with-error-body response as a defect in its own right: a server-side failure to process an upload should return a 5xx, both so that generic monitoring sees it and so that clients retry with correct backoff semantics.

Next, the two Dockerfiles need to become one. CI must build the image that ships, and the production deploy must consume that artifact rather than rebuild from a separate definition; until they are unified, any dependency change can diverge the same way this one did.

The mocked thumbnail generator should be replaced in at least one integration test by a real invocation running inside the production image, so that a missing binary fails the pipeline rather than the users. Finally, a post-deploy smoke test that performs one genuine end-to-end upload and asserts on the response body would have caught this within a minute or two of 09:12, and is worth adding independently of the other three.

# Upgrading from v2 to v3

v3 changes five things that will break existing code, and there is no codemod. What there is instead is v2.9, which emits a deprecation warning for every one of those five. The practical path is two hops rather than one: install 2.9, run your test suite with warnings made visible (`python -W error::DeprecationWarning -m pytest`, or at minimum `-W default`), fix everything it reports, and move to 3.0 only once the run is clean. Taking it in that order means your signal comes from a version that still executes your old code, rather than from a pile of `TypeError`s and `AttributeError`s raised at whatever point your test run happens to reach first.

## Python 3.10 is required

v3 drops Python 3.8 and requires 3.10 or later, so this gates everything else. If your project still runs on 3.8, note that 2.9 supports it: you can do all of the warning-fixing work on your current interpreter, get a clean run, and treat the interpreter bump as a separate change with its own review. Splitting it that way keeps a 3.10 migration from being tangled up with library API changes when something goes wrong.

## `Client` takes a config object

The two-argument constructor is gone in favour of a single `ClientConfig`. For the common case there is a helper that takes exactly the old arguments, so the change is mechanical:

```python
# v2
client = Client("https://api.example.com", token)

# v3
client = Client(ClientConfig.from_url("https://api.example.com", token))
```

If you construct clients in more than a couple of places, this is a good moment to build the config once and pass it around, since everything else that used to be a constructor keyword now lives on the config object.

## Timeouts are a `Timeout` object

A float is no longer accepted; in v3 it raises `TypeError` rather than warning, so there is no grace period once you are on 3.0. The replacement separates the two phases that the single number used to cover:

```python
# v2
timeout=30.0

# v3
timeout=Timeout(connect=5.0, read=30.0)
```

Because the old value conflated connecting and reading, this is not a straight substitution. A single 30-second budget usually meant "give up on a slow response after 30 seconds", and connection setup should fail much sooner than that, so the usual translation is a short connect and a read at or near the old number. Anywhere the old float was tuned deliberately, check what it was tuned against before you split it.

## Methods return dataclasses, not dicts

Every method that returned a `dict` now returns a typed dataclass, so `result["items"]` becomes `result.items`. This is the change most likely to slip through, because dict access spreads further than the call sites themselves: `result.get("items", [])`, `"items" in result`, `json.dumps(result)`, iteration over keys, and anything that passes a result into a function annotated for `Mapping` will all need attention. Subscripting still works in 2.9 and warns, which is what makes the intermediate step worth the trouble; the warning fires at the access, giving you the exact line. Where you were relying on `.get()` for a key that might be absent, an optional field on the dataclass will be `None` instead, so the fallback moves from the accessor to the value.

## `fetch_all()` is removed in favour of `iterate()`

This is the one change that is not just a syntax edit, because `fetch_all()` was removed for a reason: it built the entire result set in memory. `iterate()` yields pages, so the shape of the loop changes:

```python
# v2
for item in client.fetch_all():
    handle(item)

# v3
for page in client.iterate():
    for item in page:
        handle(item)
```

If you prefer a flat iterator, `itertools.chain.from_iterable(client.iterate())` gives you one without materialising anything. You can also reproduce the old behaviour exactly with `[item for page in client.iterate() for item in page]`, and that is the right move for code that calls `len()` on the result, indexes into it, or iterates it more than once. Doing so keeps the old memory profile too, so treat it as a stopgap rather than the destination.

## What you get on the other side

Three additions arrive with v3 and require no changes to adopt. `AsyncClient` mirrors the sync API for use under `asyncio`. Retries on HTTP 429 are now automatic and honour the `Retry-After` header, which means any hand-rolled retry loop around 429 should come out: leaving it in gives you two layers of backoff multiplying each other, and the outer layer will not respect the server's own guidance. Structured logging hooks let you attach request and response detail to your existing logging setup instead of parsing it back out of log strings.

## Order of work

1. Pin to 2.9 and run the test suite with deprecation warnings surfaced.
2. Fix the constructor, timeout, and attribute-access warnings, which are mechanical.
3. Rewrite `fetch_all()` call sites, which need judgement about memory and reuse.
4. Get a clean run under `-W error::DeprecationWarning`.
5. Bump the interpreter to 3.10 or later if you are not there already.
6. Move to 3.0 and remove any 429 retry logic you were carrying yourself.

# Migrating from v2 to v3

v3 changes the shape of the client's public surface in five ways, and there is no codemod. The maintainers recommend upgrading in two hops rather than one: pin to 2.9 first, which still runs your existing code but emits a `DeprecationWarning` for every construct listed below, fix the warnings until the run is clean, then bump to 3.0. The advantage is that 2.9 tells you where your call sites are, which saves you grepping for patterns like `result["items"]` that a search cannot reliably distinguish from ordinary dict access elsewhere in your code.

To make the warnings impossible to ignore while you work through them, run your suite under `python -W error::DeprecationWarning`, or add `filterwarnings = ["error::DeprecationWarning"]` to your pytest config. Turn that back off before you ship 2.9 to production if anything in your dependency tree emits warnings of its own.

## Constructing the client

The two positional arguments are gone; the constructor now takes a single config object.

```python
# v2
client = Client("https://api.example.com", token)

# v3
from mylib import Client, ClientConfig
client = Client(ClientConfig.from_url("https://api.example.com", token))
```

`ClientConfig.from_url` covers the simple case and is the mechanical replacement. If you were passing anything beyond URL and token, or if you build clients in more than two or three places, construct the config once at the edge of your application and pass it down, since that is the arrangement the new API is designed for.

## Dict returns become dataclasses

Every method that returned a `dict` now returns a typed dataclass, so key access becomes attribute access: `result["items"]` is `result.items`. This is the change with the widest blast radius, and it breaks in more ways than the obvious one. Calls to `.get("key")` with a default no longer work; use `getattr` if the field is genuinely optional, though in most cases the dataclass field exists and is `None`. Membership tests like `"items" in result` will fail, as will `**result` unpacking and passing the result straight to `json.dumps`. Where you were serializing a response, insert an explicit conversion at that boundary:

```python
import dataclasses
payload = json.dumps(dataclasses.asdict(result))
```

The upside is that a type checker can now find the rest of these for you. If you run mypy or pyright, do it after this step rather than before; the errors it reports at that point are close to a complete list of the remaining call sites.

## `fetch_all()` is removed

`fetch_all()` loaded the entire result set into memory, which is why it is gone rather than deprecated in place. `iterate()` replaces it and yields pages, not individual records, so the rewrite adds a level of nesting:

```python
# v2
for item in client.fetch_all():
    process(item)

# v3
for page in client.iterate():
    for item in page.items:
        process(item)
```

If you prefer to keep the flat loop, `itertools.chain.from_iterable(page.items for page in client.iterate())` gives you an iterator of items. What you should not do is `[item for page in client.iterate() for item in page.items]` as a reflex, since materializing the list reintroduces exactly the memory behaviour the removal was meant to fix. Code that genuinely needs the whole set at once, such as a sort across all results, is worth looking at again; often the aggregate can be computed incrementally as pages arrive.

## Timeouts

A float is no longer accepted, and v3 raises `TypeError` rather than warning, so anything you miss fails loudly at the call site.

```python
# v2
client.request(..., timeout=5.0)

# v3
from mylib import Timeout
client.request(..., timeout=Timeout(connect=5.0, read=5.0))
```

Setting both values to your old float is the safe starting point, but note that it is not an exact translation: the single float and the pair do not budget time the same way, so a request that previously fit inside the old limit can now take longer in the worst case. If you have latency budgets that depend on the timeout, treat this as a chance to set them deliberately, with a short connect timeout and a longer read timeout being the usual arrangement.

## Python 3.10 minimum

Support for 3.8 is dropped. Update `requires-python` in your packaging metadata and drop 3.8 and 3.9 from your CI matrix before you bump the library, so you find out about the runtime change separately from the API changes. Nothing in the migration requires new syntax, so you can do the interpreter bump as its own commit.

## What you get in v3

Three additions need no changes on your side, but two of them may let you delete code. Retries on 429 are now automatic and honour `Retry-After`, so if you hand-rolled a retry loop around rate limiting, remove it rather than leaving it in place; two layers of backoff will multiply your wait times and make throttling look like a hang. Structured logging hooks replace whatever you were doing to correlate requests, and are worth wiring up while you are already touching the client construction code. `AsyncClient` mirrors the sync API method for method, so an async port is largely mechanical, though it is a separate piece of work and not something to attempt in the same pass as the migration.

## Suggested order

Working through it in this sequence keeps each step verifiable. Bump the interpreter and CI matrix first, then pin 2.9 and turn deprecation warnings into errors. Fix the constructor and timeout call sites, which are mechanical and few. Then take the dict-to-dataclass conversion, leaning on a type checker once the first pass is done. Save `fetch_all()` for last, because it is the only change that may need a real decision about how your code consumes results. When the suite is clean under 2.9 with warnings as errors, moving the pin to 3.0 should be uneventful.

# Migrating from v2 to v3

## Go through v2.9 first

There is no codemod for this upgrade, so the deprecation warnings in v2.9 are the closest thing to one. Pin to 2.9, run your test suite with `-W error::DeprecationWarning`, and fix what it flags; every breaking change described below emits a warning there under the old API, which means a codebase that runs clean on 2.9 will usually run clean on 3.0 without further edits. Going straight from 2.x to 3.0 works too, but you trade a list of warnings pointing at exact call sites for a series of `TypeError`s and `AttributeError`s discovered one test run at a time.

The one change 2.9 cannot warn you about is the Python version, so settle that first.

## Python 3.10 is now the minimum

Support for 3.8 is dropped and 3.9 is not supported either; v3 requires 3.10 or later. If you are still on 3.8, do that interpreter upgrade as its own change, with its own test run, before you touch any library code. Debugging a `match` statement's absence and a changed constructor signature in the same pull request is unpleasant.

## `Client` takes a config object

The constructor no longer accepts a URL and token as positional arguments. It takes a single `ClientConfig`, and for the common case there is a helper that reproduces the old call exactly:

```python
# v2
client = Client("https://api.example.com", token)

# v3
client = Client(ClientConfig.from_url("https://api.example.com", token))
```

If you were passing extra keyword arguments to the constructor, they now belong on the config object instead, either as arguments to `ClientConfig(...)` directly or set on the instance returned by `from_url`. This is worth a moment's thought rather than a mechanical rewrite: if you construct clients in several places with slightly different options, a config object is a thing you can build once, store, and pass around, which is largely why the signature changed.

## Methods return dataclasses, not dicts

Every method that used to hand back a `dict` now returns a typed dataclass, and key access becomes attribute access:

```python
# v2
items = result["items"]
cursor = result.get("next_cursor")

# v3
items = result.items
cursor = result.next_cursor
```

The subscript form is the obvious breakage and the one the warnings will catch, but the incidental dict behaviours are what tend to survive the first pass and fail later. Anything that called `.get()` with a default, tested membership with `in`, iterated `.keys()` or `.items()`, splatted a result into a function with `**result`, or passed one straight to `json.dumps` needs rewriting. For serialisation, `dataclasses.asdict(result)` gives you the dict back. For an optional field, read the attribute and compare against `None` rather than reaching for a default, since the field is always present on the dataclass even when its value is missing.

## `fetch_all()` is gone; use `iterate()`

`fetch_all()` was removed rather than deprecated in place because its whole behaviour was the problem: it accumulated every page in memory before returning. `iterate()` yields pages instead, so the rewrite is a loop with one extra level of nesting:

```python
# v2
for item in client.fetch_all():
    handle(item)

# v3
for page in client.iterate():
    for item in page.items:
        handle(item)
```

Where the surrounding code genuinely needs the whole collection in memory, say because it sorts or counts across the full set, you can write `list(chain.from_iterable(page.items for page in client.iterate()))`. Do that knowingly, though, since it reintroduces exactly the memory profile the removal was meant to eliminate. Code that only streams through results should stay streaming.

## Timeouts are a `Timeout` object

A float is no longer accepted and no longer coerced; passing one raises `TypeError` at the call site. Connect and read timeouts are now separate values:

```python
# v2
client.request(..., timeout=30.0)

# v3
client.request(..., timeout=Timeout(connect=5.0, read=30.0))
```

Splitting one number into two is a judgment call, not a substitution, because the old float bounded the whole operation while the new values bound two different phases. A short connect timeout and a longer read timeout is the usual shape: failing to establish a connection is nearly always a fast, permanent failure, whereas a slow response is often a slow success. Carrying your old value over as the read timeout and choosing something small for connect will preserve behaviour closely enough for most callers.

## What you get in return

`AsyncClient` mirrors the synchronous API with the same config object and the same return types, so the migration to async, if you want it, is mostly a matter of awaiting calls and writing `async for page in client.iterate()`. Rate limiting is now handled for you: v3 retries automatically on a 429 and honours the `Retry-After` header. Check whether you have your own 429 handling, because retry loops compose badly, and a hand-written backoff wrapped around a client that already backs off will wait far longer than either layer intends. Removing yours is usually the right move. Finally, structured logging hooks let you attach a handler that receives request and response records as objects rather than formatted strings, which is worth wiring up while you are already touching client construction.

Your skepticism is reasonable, though pool exhaustion is at least the right *shape* of hypothesis. The most informative fact you have is that the hang lands on a different test each time, which almost rules out a bug in the test that hangs. A test that deadlocks on its own logic hangs in the same place every time. A varying victim means something accumulates across the run, or some race resolves badly, and whichever test is holding the bag when the threshold is crossed takes the blame.

The accumulation story is the family pool exhaustion belongs to, and it generalises: a test errors out on a path that skips cleanup, a connection or transaction or file descriptor or worker thread is never returned, and the pool shrinks run by run until a checkout blocks forever because nobody set an acquire timeout. The same shape covers leaked database transactions specifically, which are nastier than plain exhaustion: a session left idle in transaction holds row or table locks, and the next test that touches those rows waits on `lock_timeout`, which in Postgres defaults to unlimited. Under CI's different timing and ordering, a different test gets caught each run.

The second family has nothing to do with your code's resource discipline and everything to do with CI's network. A blocking read on a socket whose peer has quietly vanished will wait forever unless something imposes a deadline. Containerised CI is unusually good at producing vanished peers: NAT conntrack entries expiring on idle connections so subsequent packets are blackholed rather than reset, a service container OOM-killed mid-suite, a DNS lookup stalling, or a connect to an external dependency with no connect timeout. This explains "never locally" far better than a leak does, since your laptop has a loopback interface and no NAT table in between.

Third, there are missed-wakeup races. Any test that registers a listener and then waits for an event has a window where the event can arrive first; if it does, the wait never completes. CI machines are usually slower and more contended than your laptop, so orderings that never occur locally occur at some low rate there. A 5% failure rate across a few hundred tests is a very small per-test window, which is exactly what this kind of race looks like.

Finally, be suspicious of the observation itself. If your runner buffers output, the last test name printed is not the test that hung; it is the last one that flushed. Relatedly, a subprocess whose stderr pipe fills while nobody drains it will block on write forever, and which test triggers that depends on which one happens to be verbose that run.

To tell these apart, stop reasoning about them and capture state at the moment of the hang. Set a per-test or per-suite timeout comfortably below the CI job timeout, and on expiry dump stacks for every thread or task, the pool's active/idle/waiting counts, `ss -tanp` for socket states, open fd count, and on the database side `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_locks` including `wait_event_type`. One such dump usually ends the argument: a stack sitting in `pool.acquire` is exhaustion; a stack in a socket read with no live peer is the network story; a session showing idle in transaction while another waits on a lock is a leaked transaction; all threads parked on your own mutexes is a genuine deadlock.

Two cheap experiments are worth running while you wire that up. Shrink the pool to one or two connections: if the hang rate jumps toward every run, your colleague is right and you've confirmed it in an afternoon; if the rate is unchanged, exhaustion is essentially falsified. Then run the suite with a single worker: if the hang disappears, the cause is cross-test interference or contention, and you can bisect by replaying the same random seed and trimming the prefix until the hang stops following a particular predecessor test.

Independently of diagnosis, put deadlines on everything that can block: pool acquire, socket connect and read, `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` on the database, and the test runner's own per-test limit. Timeouts convert an opaque hung job into a stack trace at the point of blocking, so the next occurrence tells you what the previous twenty could not. Reproducing locally becomes plausible too once you constrain the environment the way CI does, running the suite with `--cpus=1` and a bit of injected latency and loss.

Three facts in your description carry most of the diagnostic weight, and it's worth separating them before reaching for any specific cause. The suite hangs rather than fails, which means something is blocked waiting on an event that will never arrive, and somewhere in the stack a timeout is missing or infinite. The location moves between runs, which argues against a single defective test and toward either shared state that leaks across tests or a timing window that opens sporadically. And it only happens in CI, which points at the axes where CI actually differs from your laptop: parallelism and core count, cgroup CPU and memory limits, container networking, and service dependencies that live at the end of a bridge network instead of on localhost.

Connection pool exhaustion is a reasonable guess but it's the guess everyone makes, because it's the one everybody has been burned by once. It has a specific signature you can check against your data. A leak accumulates, so the hang should cluster in the later part of the run and correlate with the cumulative number of tests executed rather than with which test it lands on, and raising the pool size should push the hang later without removing it. It also requires that your pool has no acquire timeout configured, because a pool with a two-second acquire timeout produces a loud error and a stack trace rather than silence. That last point is a thirty-second falsification: read the pool config, and if there's a finite acquire timeout on it, the hypothesis is dead and you've saved yourself a week.

The alternatives worth holding in mind fall into a few families. Mutual blocking is the first: two parallel workers touching the same rows or tables, one of them leaving a transaction open on an error path so it sits idle-in-transaction holding a lock, while another blocks forever on a truncate or an alter because no lock timeout is set. Most engines detect true deadlock cycles and abort, but a plain lock wait with no timeout hangs indefinitely, and which test gets caught depends on interleaving, which explains the moving target precisely. A close cousin is thread pool starvation, where a bounded executor runs tasks that block waiting on other tasks needing the same executor, something that only bites once concurrency happens to reach the boundary. Lost wakeups are the second family: a condition signalled before the waiter began waiting, an unawaited promise, or, in integration tests specifically, one test consuming a message that another test was waiting for because they share a queue or topic without per-test namespacing. The third family is blackholed I/O, and it deserves particular attention given the CI-only pattern. On your laptop you talk to a service on localhost, so when the peer dies you get an immediate connection reset. In CI, across a bridge network or NAT to a service container that was OOM-killed or restarted, packets go into a hole and a client with an infinite read timeout waits until the job is cancelled. The fourth is the harness itself rather than your code: a child process whose stdout pipe fills its buffer and blocks on write while the parent waits for exit without draining it, or a leaked non-daemon thread that keeps the runner alive after the last test finished. Both are worth ruling in or out early by establishing whether the hang is inside a test or after the last one reported. Finally there's infrastructure, meaning CPU throttling under a cgroup quota, memory pressure turning into a GC death spiral that looks like a stall, a preempted spot instance, or log streaming stalling while the job underneath is fine.

The way to tell these apart is to stop trying to reproduce it and instead make the next occurrence self-diagnosing, because at one in twenty you'll get an instance within a day or two of merging instrumentation. Set a job timeout comfortably below the CI hard limit, and on expiry, before anything is killed, capture a full thread or goroutine dump of the test process, the state of every socket via `ss -tanp`, open file descriptors, and on the database side the contents of `pg_stat_activity` including state, wait_event and transaction start time, plus `pg_locks` joined to show blocked and blocking pairs. Add broker queue depth and consumer counts if a broker is involved, cgroup throttling counters, and `dmesg` for OOM kills. The mechanism differs by runtime: SIGQUIT for a JVM or Go process, `py-spy dump` against the pid for Python, `--report-on-signal` for Node. That single artifact discriminates almost everything above. Every thread parked in acquire means the pool. One thread in a socket read on a connection whose peer is gone means a missing timeout and probably a vanished container. An idle-in-transaction session with a waiter behind it means the lock story. Nothing running anywhere and a full pipe means the harness.

Alongside that, a few cheap experiments narrow the space without waiting. Run the integration suite with a single worker over enough runs to matter; if the hang disappears, it's cross-test interference rather than a per-test defect, and doubling the workers instead should make it more frequent, which also gives you a faster feedback loop. Add short timeouts everywhere you can, on socket reads, pool acquisition, statements and lock waits, since converting a hang into an error with a stack trace at the point of blockage costs you nothing and buys evidence on every future occurrence. Log a timestamped line at each test's start and end so you can see the run position of the hang and check whether it drifts later as the suite grows. And run the actual CI image locally, pinned to one or two cores with the same memory limit and the same service-container topology, because "never hangs locally" usually stops being true once the container network and the resource limits are part of the picture, and identifying which of those two restores the failure is itself the answer. Worth checking in parallel whether the failures correlate with a particular runner host, shard, or time of day, since a single sick machine or a noisy neighbour is a common and easily missed explanation for a stable one-in-twenty rate.

Two facts in your description do most of the diagnostic work, and they point away from the pool theory as stated. The first is that it lands on a different test each time, which means the fault almost certainly isn't in any test's own logic but in something shared: a resource that accumulates across the run, a piece of global state one test leaves behind for whichever test runs next, or a race that any test can lose given the wrong interleaving. The second is that it never happens locally, which usually means the CI machine differs in a way your code is quietly sensitive to, most often core count, latency, or memory pressure rather than anything about the code path itself.

Connection pool exhaustion is a member of the first family and worth taking seriously, but it makes a prediction you can check almost for free. A leak drains the pool monotonically, so hangs should cluster toward the end of the run rather than scattering uniformly across it. If you plot where in the suite each of your failures landed and the distribution looks flat, exhaustion in the simple sense is unlikely. It's also worth noting that an exhausted pool is very often the symptom rather than the disease: one operation hangs while holding a connection, and twenty tests later the pool is empty and everything blocks on acquire. The hang you observe is then several minutes downstream of the actual bug.

The candidate I'd weight most heavily given "never locally" is thread pool or event loop starvation caused by a smaller CI machine. If any pool is sized from the CPU count, your laptop's twelve cores and the runner's two produce very different concurrency limits, and code that blocks a worker while waiting on work that must be executed by that same pool deadlocks only once the required concurrency exceeds the pool size. This reproduces reliably under `taskset -c 0,1` or `docker run --cpuset-cpus=2`, which makes it cheap to confirm or eliminate.

Close behind is cross-test state leakage, which the random ordering many suites use would explain the "different test every time" pattern neatly. A test that leaves a transaction open holds locks, and the next test's truncate or migration blocks behind it forever, since a plain lock wait is not a deadlock cycle and the database's deadlock detector will never fire. Frozen or mocked clocks do the same thing in a different register: a test freezes time globally, doesn't restore it, and something downstream waits on a timeout that can no longer elapse. In both cases the culprit is a pair of tests, not one, so the useful thing to record is which test ran immediately *before* the hang, along with the ordering seed.

Then there is the family of missing timeouts meeting a different network. A TCP connect to a host whose packets are being dropped by CI egress rules, a DNS lookup with no deadline, a dependent service container that came up slowly or was OOM-killed and is no longer accepting connections: locally each of these is loopback and instant, in CI each can block indefinitely if no timeout is set.
