The way to collapse all of this from speculation into one observation is to capture a stack dump at the moment of the hang instead of reasoning from the outside. Set the CI job timeout below the platform's kill timeout and use it to signal the process rather than terminate it: `timeout -s QUIT` gives you all goroutines in Go and a thread dump in the JVM, `py-spy dump --pid` works on a live Python process without cooperation, Node gives you a report on SIGUSR2 with `--report-on-signal`. Pair that with `ss -tanp` for socket states and a query against the database's own view of active and idle-in-transaction sessions. One good dump will tell you whether you're parked in a pool acquire, a lock wait, a socket read, or a condition variable, and those four answers correspond to four different bugs.

While you're waiting for that, make the hang fail loudly. Put an acquire timeout on the pool, a statement and lock timeout on the database, and read and connect timeouts on every client, so the next occurrence is a stack trace rather than silence. Setting pool size to one with a short acquire timeout will also settle the original hypothesis in a single run: if the theory is right, the failure becomes immediate and deterministic, and if the suite passes normally, you can stop arguing about it.

Your instinct is worth trusting, because the shape of the evidence constrains the answer more than the pool guess does. "Different test each time" is the important part: it argues strongly against a bug in any particular test and toward something shared, and it splits into two quite different stories. Either something accumulates across the run and the victim is simply whichever test asks for the exhausted resource next, or every test is running the same risky pattern and occasionally loses a race. Connection pool exhaustion is one member of the first family, but so is any leaked handle: unclosed HTTP agents, file descriptors, undrained child-process pipes, orphaned transactions. A third possibility that people usually forget is that the test named in the output is not where the process is stuck at all. Most runners report a test as started and then never report a result, so a hang in global teardown, in a reporter flushing to a socket, or in an `afterEach` hook will be attributed to whatever happened to be in flight.

The reason it only happens in CI is almost never mysterious: CI machines have fewer cores, contended IO, and no TTY. A race whose losing window is microseconds on your laptop becomes milliseconds on a throttled two-core container, and something that never lost in a thousand local runs loses one time in twenty there. Non-TTY output changes buffering too, which matters more than it sounds: if any test spawns a subprocess and doesn't drain its stdout, the child blocks forever once the 64KB pipe buffer fills, and it fills only when logging is verbose, which is exactly the CI configuration. Database locks behave the same way. Postgres has no default lock timeout, so one test that leaves an idle transaction holding a row lock will hang the next writer indefinitely rather than erroring, and under parallel workers on a shared database that's a genuine deadlock rather than exhaustion.

Rather than reasoning further about which of these it is, the decisive move is to get a stack out of the hung process, because that single observation collapses the whole space at once. The problem today is that CI kills the job at its own timeout and you get nothing. Fix that first: set a per-test or per-suite timeout comfortably below the job timeout, and install a signal handler that dumps state before the process dies. On the JVM that's `jstack` or `kill -3`; in Go, SIGQUIT already dumps every goroutine; in Python, `faulthandler.register(SIGUSR1)` or an out-of-band `py-spy dump --pid`; in Node you want an async-resource dump along the lines of `why-is-node-running`, since a plain stack will just show an idle event loop. While you're at it, have the same handler shell out for `ss -tanp` and, if a database is involved, `SELECT state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query FROM pg_stat_activity`. A socket stuck in a read, a thread parked on a pool acquire, and a backend waiting on a lock look nothing alike, and you will know within one hang which you have.

There are two cheap experiments worth running in parallel with that. Log the ordinal position of each test as it starts, so that when a hang happens you know whether it was the 30th test or the 300th; accumulation bias toward the end of the run is the signature of a leak, and a uniform distribution across positions effectively rules the leak family out. Then run a nightly job with parallelism forced to one. If the hang survives that, it's a single test interacting badly with a slow environment, and cross-test interference is off the table.

As for the pool theory specifically, it is cheap to falsify rather than argue about. Configure an acquire timeout on the pool, a few seconds, and a `lock_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on the database side. If pool exhaustion or a lock is the mechanism, the next occurrence stops being a hang and becomes a loud error with a stack at the point of acquisition, which is most of the diagnosis handed to you. If the run still hangs silently with those timeouts in place, the block isn't happening anywhere your pool or your database can see it, and you should be looking at sockets without timeouts, subprocess pipes, and event-loop-level races instead.

Start with the fact that's doing the most work: the hang lands on a different test every time. A bug in one test's logic would cluster. When the victim is essentially arbitrary, the thing failing is machinery shared by all of them, and whichever test is holding the baton when the shared thing wedges takes the blame. Connection pool exhaustion fits that shape, which is presumably why it was suggested, but so do half a dozen other mechanisms, and the useful move is to narrow by shape rather than to argue about which story sounds best.

The other constraint worth taking seriously is that it hangs rather than fails. Something is waiting on something else with no bound on how long it will wait. That is a much smaller set of places than "anything that could go wrong," and it's worth enumerating where unbounded waits actually live in an integration suite. A connection pool with no checkout timeout is one, and note the corollary: if your pool does have a checkout timeout of thirty seconds, then a job that sits for twenty minutes is not pool exhaustion, and you can retire that hypothesis in five minutes by reading the pool config. Database lock waits are a second, and they're nastier than deadlocks because a real deadlock gets detected and one transaction gets aborted with a clear error, whereas a plain lock wait in Postgres blocks forever unless someone set `lock_timeout`, which almost nobody does. The classic version is a fixture doing a `TRUNCATE` or a DDL migration queued behind a session left `idle in transaction` by an earlier test that didn't clean up. Sockets are a third: a connection to a service container that established and then had its peer die without sending a RST will sit in `ESTABLISHED` until TCP keepalive notices, which by default is a couple of hours. Pipes are a fourth, and this one is very specifically a CI bug: a child process writes more than the pipe buffer to stdout while the parent is blocked waiting for the child to exit instead of draining it, and both sides sleep forever. Locally you have a terminal or different verbosity settings and never fill the buffer. In-process synchronisation is the fifth, where a lost wakeup, a promise never settled on an error path, or an `await` on a queue nobody will push to hangs a worker under an interleaving that only a slow, contended machine produces.

Three measurements separate most of that, and they're cheap. The first is whether the machine is busy or idle while it's hung. Idle means genuinely blocked on a wait, which points at the list above; busy means livelock, thrash, or retry storm, which points somewhere quite different. The second is where in the run the hang falls. Anything driven by a leak, including pool exhaustion, file descriptors, and orphaned transactions, accumulates, so the hang should be biased toward the end of the run. If you log each test's ordinal position and the hang positions come out roughly uniform over twenty samples, leak-style exhaustion is in real trouble as an explanation. The third is whether the hanging tests are random or all drawn from one family, such as everything that spawns a subprocess or everything that touches the message broker. People often report "a different test each time" when what's true is "a different test from the same class each time," and that class names the shared machinery directly.

The change that pays for itself before any of this is making the next hang produce evidence. Right now CI presumably hits a job timeout and gets killed with nothing to show. Wrap the integration run in a watchdog set below the CI timeout that, on firing, captures state and then kills things: thread or goroutine stacks from every process in the tree (`SIGQUIT` for a JVM, `py-spy dump --pid`, `SIGQUIT` for Go, `SIGUSR1` plus the inspector for Node), `ps auxf` so you can see the process tree and who is a child of what, `ss -tanp` for socket states and queue depths, `pg_stat_activity` including `wait_event_type`, `wait_event`, `state`, and `query` for every backend, your pool's gauges, and `/proc/pressure/*` if you're on a recent kernel. One captured hang read this way usually ends the investigation outright, because a stack trace showing a thread parked in `read()` on a socket to your Kafka container is not something anyone needs to theorise about.

While you wait for that, you can attack the frequency directly instead of accepting one in twenty. The reason it never hangs locally is a list of concrete differences, and each one is a knob you can turn to amplify. Locally you likely have more cores and no cgroup quota, so run the suite under `--cpus=0.5` or with a CPU stress load beside it; if the rate climbs sharply, you're looking at a timing or interleaving problem rather than a resource one. Locally you often run a subset rather than the whole suite in one process, so try running only the last third of the suite and see whether the hang survives; if it needs the full prefix, something is accumulating. Locally your test order may be fixed, so shuffle with a recorded seed, and when a hang occurs, re-run with the same seed. If it reproduces deterministically, the cause is cross-test state and ordering and you can bisect the prefix; if it doesn't, the nondeterminism is genuinely in the scheduler or the network and the prefix is incidental. Those three knobs, CPU pressure, prefix length, and ordering seed, span most of the hypothesis space between them, and any one of them showing a strong effect tells you more than a week of reading test code.

I'd split it, but not along the line your team is arguing about. The choice isn't really "one Postgres" versus "one append-only store"; it's hot versus cold, and the two halves of your requirement pull in opposite directions hard enough that trying to serve both from one home is what's making the decision feel contentious.

Start with the volume, because I suspect it's being used as an argument in a way it doesn't support. Two million events a day is about twenty-three writes per second on average, maybe a hundred at peak. Postgres will not notice that. Nobody should be choosing an architecture here on write throughput. The actual number that matters is the cumulative one: seven years at that rate is roughly five billion rows, and at a realistic 500 bytes to a kilobyte per event once you include a JSON payload, you are looking at somewhere between three and eight terabytes with indexes. That volume in your application database is what hurts, and it hurts in a specific and underappreciated place, which is recovery. Your application data probably restores in minutes. Bolt a multi-terabyte audit archive onto the same cluster and your disaster recovery time is now governed by data that no user-facing request will ever touch. You also inherit the archive in every base backup, every replica rebuild, and every major-version upgrade rehearsal, and you inherit its autovacuum and bloat behaviour on the same instance that serves your checkout path.

Against that, the same-database camp has one argument that is genuinely strong and usually gets stated badly. If the audit row is written in the same transaction as the mutation it describes, then an action cannot commit without its audit record. Ship events over the wire to a separate store and you have introduced a delivery problem: at-least-once gives you duplicates, at-most-once gives you gaps, and gaps in an audit log are exactly the thing compliance cares about. Any design that has the application POST to an external audit service and hope is worse than keeping it all in Postgres, whatever the operational cost.

So write into Postgres, into a table declaratively range-partitioned by month, in the same transaction as the change it records. Then run a mover that ages partitions out after a hot window of ninety days or so, detaching each one and writing it to object storage as Parquet under an object-lock retention policy. Recent events, which is what support actually opens, stay in the database where you can join them freely. The seven-year tail lives somewhere that costs a few dollars a terabyte per month, is genuinely immutable in a way an auditor will accept rather than in the approximated way that revoking UPDATE and DELETE grants gives you, and is queryable when you need it through Athena or DuckDB without being on the critical path for anything.

The join requirement mostly dissolves under a change you want to make regardless. An audit event should record the actor's identity as it was at the moment of the event: email, display name, role, tenant, all denormalised into the row. If you instead join to the live users table you will eventually show an investigator the wrong answer, because the user was renamed, changed roles, or was deleted in the two years since. Once those fields are on the event, "occasionally join against user records" turns out to mean "occasionally look up a user by id in a second query," which works fine across a store boundary.

Two things would change my recommendation. If your compliance regime is something like SEC 17a-4 that demands true WORM media, the archive half stops being optional and the hot window should be as short as your support workflow tolerates. Conversely, if the obligation is only seven years retained with retrieval measured in days rather than seconds, lean further cold: shrink the hot window to thirty days and stop worrying about query ergonomics on the tail entirely. Worth pinning down which of those you're actually subject to before the team spends more time on it, because it settles more of the argument than any of the technical points do.

I'd separate the storage without separating the technology: run the audit log in its own Postgres database, ideally its own instance, rather than as another set of tables alongside application data. That keeps SQL, your existing operational knowledge, and the ability to join, while cutting the couplings that make people nervous about the single-database option.

The volume argument is mostly a red herring in both directions. Two million events a day is about twenty-three writes per second averaged out, maybe a few hundred at peak, which is nothing for Postgres and no reason to reach for a specialised store. The pressure comes from retention rather than throughput. Seven years is roughly five billion rows, and depending on payload size that is several terabytes before indexes. If that sits in your application database it dominates your backups, your restore time, your logical dumps, and your major-version upgrades, which means the recovery time objective for the data your business actually runs on gets tied to hauling around log data nobody is querying during an outage. Separation buys you the freedom to back the two up on different schedules with different retention and different urgency.

The append-only camp is usually reaching for something real, but it is worth naming precisely, because it is not immutability in the abstract. You can get append-only semantics inside Postgres by granting a writer role INSERT only, revoking UPDATE and DELETE, and adding a trigger that raises on modification; if you need tamper evidence rather than tamper resistance, hash-chain each row against its predecessor and periodically sign the head. What none of that survives is a superuser on the same instance. If your compliance posture requires that the people who administer the application database cannot rewrite audit history, you need separation of duties enforced by separate credentials on separate infrastructure, and a separate schema in the same cluster will not give you that. Decide whether your auditors care about this, because it is the one argument that genuinely forces the split.

On the join requirement, I'd push back on the premise a little. Joining a three-year-old audit event against the live users table tells you what the actor is called today, not what they were called or what permissions they held at the time, and for support investigations that difference is occasionally the whole question. Denormalise the actor's identifying attributes into the event at write time: user id, email as it stood, role, tenant, whatever the investigation needs. That is better auditing regardless of where you store it, and it dissolves most of the join requirement as a side effect. For the residual cases, postgres_fdw across the two databases handles ad-hoc support queries perfectly well at the volumes a human investigation generates.

Whichever way you go, partition the audit table by time from day one, monthly giving you eighty-four partitions across the retention window. Keep twelve to eighteen months hot and roll older partitions out to Parquet in object storage with a documented retrieval path; compliance regimes almost always accept hours-to-retrieve for multi-year-old records, though confirm yours does before you build around it.

Two things would change my recommendation. If your regulator names immutable media specifically, in the SEC 17a-4 sense, then the system of record has to be object storage with object-lock and Postgres becomes an index over it. Conversely, if you have no operational capacity for a second instance, a single database with partitioning, a restricted writer role, and a written plan to split later is defensible, because partitioning is the decision that is painful to retrofit at five billion rows and the split is not.

I'd keep it in Postgres, but not in the shape either side of your team is likely arguing for: same cluster, its own database or at minimum its own schema with its own roles, time-partitioned, and with anything older than roughly eighteen months detached and shipped to immutable object storage. That gives you most of the integrity and cost properties the append-only camp wants without surrendering the transactional and relational properties the other camp is defending.

Start with the numbers, because they're less alarming than they sound in one direction and more alarming in another. Two million events a day is about twenty-three writes a second averaged, maybe a few hundred at peak, which is nothing for Postgres; throughput is not your problem and nobody should be choosing an architecture around it. Seven years of it is roughly 5.1 billion rows, and at five hundred bytes to a kilobyte per event with a JSON payload you're looking at several terabytes before indexes. The cost of that isn't in writing it, it's in carrying it: backup windows, point-in-time-restore times measured in hours, autovacuum freeze pressure on a table that never gets updated but still has to be frozen against transaction ID wraparound, and major-version upgrades that now have to drag the whole thing along. Those costs land on your application database's operational envelope, which is why the instinct to move audit somewhere else is a sound one even though the reasoning usually offered for it is not.

The strongest argument for staying in Postgres is one that often goes unstated. If the audit row is written in the same transaction as the change it describes, you cannot get a business change without its audit record, and you cannot get an audit record for a change that rolled back. Ship events to a separate store over the network and you have re-created an exactly-once delivery problem, which in practice means an outbox table in Postgres anyway plus a relay process, plus monitoring for relay lag, plus a reconciliation job for when the relay silently falls behind during an incident. For a log whose entire value is that a regulator or an investigator can trust it, an eventually-consistent pipeline with a queue in the middle is a worse guarantee than a foreign key.

The join requirement is weaker than it looks, and worth interrogating before it drives the decision. A support investigation that joins a five-year-old audit event to the current user record is arguably producing a wrong answer, because the user's email, role and permissions have changed since the event happened. Audit events should carry a snapshot of the actor's identity at write time: id, email, role, tenant, whatever the investigation needs. Once you denormalise that way, the thing you actually need is not a join but an indexed lookup on actor_id, which works identically whether the data lives beside your users table or in Parquet files on S3. Keeping the live join available for recent data is still convenient, and that's what the hot partitions are for.

On tamper-evidence, you can get most of what a dedicated append-only store sells you. Revoke UPDATE and DELETE from every role including the application's, so the only grant on the table is INSERT. Hash-chain the rows, each one covering the previous row's hash, so any excision or edit is detectable rather than merely discouraged. Ship archived partitions to object storage with a WORM policy and a retention lock that your own operators cannot clear. What you cannot get is custody by a third party, and if your compliance regime specifically demands that the audit log sit outside the control of the people who run the application, then the decision is already made for you and no amount of Postgres tuning changes it.

So my honest read is that this is a partitioning and tiering problem that has been framed as a storage-engine problem. I'd flip to a genuinely separate store in two cases: if a regulator requires custody separation, or if your audit consumers turn out to be analytics-shaped, scanning hundreds of millions of rows to answer aggregate questions rather than pulling up one user's history. Neither is described in what you've laid out, and the seven-year retention that makes the volume scary is cold compliance data that almost never gets read, which is exactly what the archival tier is for.

I'd go with a separate append-only store as the system of record, but have the events originate in Postgres and keep a rolling recent window there. That's a definite architecture rather than a compromise, and the ordering matters: the archive is authoritative for compliance, the Postgres table is a queryable cache of the last few months.

The strongest reason to write audit events into Postgres first has nothing to do with joins. It's atomicity. If the audit write goes directly to a separate store, you own the dual-write problem: the business transaction commits and the audit event is lost, or the event is written and the transaction rolls back. Both failures are exactly the kind an auditor will ask about, and neither is fixable after the fact. Writing the event in the same transaction as the change it describes gives you the invariant you actually want, which is that an audit event exists if and only if the thing happened. From there, shipping to the archive is an asynchronous, retryable, idempotent job driven off logical decoding or an outbox table, and a failure in that pipeline delays the archive rather than corrupting the record.

The join argument is weaker than it feels. Joining a five-year-old audit event to today's user row tells you the user's current email and role, not the ones in effect when the event was recorded, so for support investigations and especially for anything evidentiary the join is quietly giving you the wrong answer. Audit events should carry denormalized copies of the identifying fields at write time: actor id, email as it then was, role, tenant, IP, session. Once events are self-contained, the join you genuinely need is against recent events for live investigations, and a ninety-day to twelve-month hot window in Postgres covers essentially all of that.

Keeping all seven years in the application database is where it goes wrong. Two million a day is only about twenty-five writes a second, so throughput is a non-issue; the problem is accumulated size. You're looking at roughly five billion rows and several terabytes with indexes, and that mass lands on operations you care about for a completely different reason. Your backups get slower, your restore time balloons, your major-version upgrade window stretches, and your recovery objective for customer-facing data is now hostage to a table nobody queries. Cold audit data in object storage as partitioned Parquet costs a small fraction of provisioned database storage and doesn't participate in any of those operations.

There's also a separation-of-duties point that carries real weight with auditors. If the log lives in the database the application writes to, the application's credentials can in principle rewrite history, and so can anyone with production database access. You can narrow that with a dedicated role, revoked UPDATE and DELETE, and triggers, but the mitigation is only as strong as the people holding superuser. A write-once store with object-lock or equivalent, plus a hash chain over events so any gap or edit is detectable, gives you an answer to "how do you know this wasn't altered" that doesn't depend on trusting your own operators.

Concretely: partition the Postgres audit table by month, keep somewhere between three and twelve months, and drop old partitions rather than deleting rows. Stream to the archive continuously, verify by reconciling counts and hash-chain heads per partition before dropping anything, and give support a query path that hits Postgres for the hot window and the archive engine for older material. Most investigations will never touch the archive.

The case for staying single-database is that this pipeline is real work and a thing that can rot if nobody owns it. If your team can't staff it, a partitioned Postgres table will survive seven years at this volume, and you'd be choosing operational drag over a system you can't maintain, which is a defensible trade. I'd revisit that immediately if event volume grows by an order of magnitude, if payloads get large, or if a customer contract starts specifying tamper-evidence, because any of those turns the drag into a genuine constraint.

I'd keep it in Postgres, but not as one undifferentiated seven-year table sitting next to your application tables, and I'd say the split on your team is probably a disagreement about two separable questions that have been fused into one.

The strongest argument for co-location is transactional integrity of the write. If the audit insert happens in the same transaction as the change it describes, the audit record exists if and only if the change committed, and you get that guarantee for free from the database. Ship to a separate store and you are dual-writing: the application change commits, the network call to the audit service fails, and now you have an unlogged privileged action, which is precisely the case an auditor cares about. The usual fix is an outbox table in Postgres plus a shipper process, but notice what that costs you. You are now writing to Postgres anyway, running a relay, and operating a second system, and you have bought nothing that Postgres wasn't already giving you. At two million events a day you are averaging around twenty-three inserts per second, so perhaps a couple of hundred at peak. That is not a volume that pushes Postgres anywhere near its limits; append-only tables with no updates are also the friendliest possible workload for autovacuum.

The join requirement is a weaker argument than it looks, and I'd examine it before leaning on it. An audit event from 2019 should record the actor's email, role and display name as they were in 2019, denormalized into the event row, because joining to the current user table tells you who that person is today rather than who they were when they did the thing. Once you denormalize the identity fields you need, the residual value of a live join is convenience during investigations, not correctness. Keep the user id as a plain column with no foreign key, since you do not want a user deletion to cascade into your audit trail or to be blocked by it.

Where I'd side with the separate-store camp is on everything the word "separate" is standing in for. Put the audit tables in their own schema with their own role. Grant the application role INSERT and nothing else, and revoke UPDATE and DELETE explicitly, so append-only is enforced by the database rather than by convention. That gets you most of what people imagine they're buying from an append-only product. Shipping to a different system does not by itself make data immutable; permissions and storage-level write-once controls do.

Then partition by month and stop keeping all seven years hot. Rough sizing: at a kilobyte per event you're looking at about two gigabytes a day, three-quarters of a terabyte a year, five terabytes plus index overhead across the retention window. Postgres can hold that, but you'll feel it in the places people forget to check: restore time when you need to recover application data, the length of your point-in-time recovery window, the cost of provisioned SSD on your primary, and the initial sync time for a new replica. Keep twelve to eighteen months attached, which covers essentially every support investigation, and detach older partitions on a schedule, exporting them to Parquet in object storage with a lifecycle policy and object lock for the remainder of the seven years. Compressed columnar files will hold the whole archive in a few hundred gigabytes, cost almost nothing, and stay queryable through DuckDB or Athena when someone genuinely needs 2021. The one discipline this requires is testing the read path for archived data before you need it, because an archive nobody has ever restored from is not an archive.

Two things would change my answer. If your compliance regime names an independent, externally attested system rather than describing controls and retention periods, then the regulator has made the decision for you and the engineering tradeoff is moot; worth reading the actual control language rather than someone's summary of it. And if your threat model includes an attacker who has compromised the application database and you need the audit trail to survive that, co-location fails by construction, though the cheaper answer there is usually hash-chaining the events and periodically anchoring the chain head somewhere the database cannot reach, rather than moving the whole store.

So: one database, separate schema and role, INSERT-only grants, monthly partitions, eighteen months online, the rest in object storage under lock. You keep the transactional write guarantee, you keep support investigations easy, and you get the isolation the other half of the team is actually asking for without operating a second system to get it.

# tug

`tug` pushes a local directory to an S3-compatible bucket. It is deliberately one-way: local is the source of truth, the remote is a copy, and nothing ever travels back down. On each run it compares every local file against the corresponding remote object and uploads only those whose size or modification time differ, so a second push over an unchanged tree costs little more than the listing calls.

## Installation

With a Go toolchain (1.21 or newer):

```
go install github.com/yourorg/tug/cmd/tug@latest
```

Or download a prebuilt binary for your platform from the releases page, then put it somewhere on your `PATH`:

```
curl -sSL https://github.com/yourorg/tug/releases/latest/download/tug_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
sudo mv tug /usr/local/bin/
```

## Quick start

```
tug status ./site s3://my-bucket/site      # what would change
tug push --dry-run ./site s3://my-bucket/site
tug push ./site s3://my-bucket/site
```

## Credentials

`tug` looks for credentials in `~/.tug/credentials` first, and falls back to the environment if the file is absent or the requested profile is not in it. The file is INI-formatted and may hold several profiles, selected with `--profile`:

```ini
[default]
access_key_id = AKIAEXAMPLE
secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
endpoint = https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
region = us-east-1

[backblaze]
access_key_id = 002abc
secret_access_key = K002xyz
endpoint = https://s3.us-west-004.backblazeb2.com
region = us-west-004
```

The equivalent environment variables are `TUG_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `TUG_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `TUG_ENDPOINT` and `TUG_REGION`; the standard `AWS_`-prefixed names are read too, so an existing AWS environment usually works without any configuration. Keep the credentials file at mode `0600`, since `tug` refuses to read it if it is group- or world-readable.

## Ignoring files

If a `.tugignore` file sits at the root of the directory being pushed, its patterns are applied to every candidate path. The syntax is gitignore's, including negation with `!`, directory-only patterns with a trailing slash, and `**` for arbitrary depth:

```
node_modules/
*.log
.DS_Store
!important.log
```

Ignored files are never uploaded and are not reported as differences by `status`. They are also invisible to `verify`, so a file excluded after it has already been pushed will simply be left in place on the remote.

## Commands

`tug push <local-dir> <s3-url>` performs the synchronisation. Each file is compared against the remote object's size and last-modified time, and one that matches on both is skipped. Pass `--dry-run` to print the upload plan and exit without touching the bucket, which is worth doing on any tree you have not pushed before.

`tug status <local-dir> <s3-url>` reports what a push would do without performing it. Unlike `--dry-run` it exits with status 1 when differences exist, which makes it usable as a check in CI or a pre-deploy hook.

`tug verify <local-dir> <s3-url>` compares content rather than metadata. It fetches each object's ETag and checks it against the local file's MD5, catching corruption and partial uploads that the size-and-mtime heuristic cannot see. Run it periodically rather than on every push, for reasons covered under limitations below.

Flags common to all three commands:

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--profile <name>` | Credentials profile to use (default `default`) |
| `--endpoint <url>` | Override the endpoint from the profile |
| `--concurrency <n>` | Parallel transfers or checks (default 8) |
| `--verbose` | Log every file considered, not just those acted on |
| `--quiet` | Suppress everything except errors |

## Limitations

There is no delete propagation. A file removed locally stays in the bucket forever, so `tug` is well suited to append-mostly trees such as build artefacts, backups and static sites with stable paths, and poorly suited to mirroring a directory you prune. If you need the remote cleaned up, do it out of band.

Uploads are single-part, which caps individual files at the S3 limit of 5 GB. A larger file is reported as an error and skipped, and the rest of the push continues.

`verify` is slow on large buckets because it issues a request per object to read the ETag, with no way to batch them. On a bucket of a few thousand objects this is unremarkable; on hundreds of thousands it will take a long time and generate a corresponding number of billable requests. Raising `--concurrency` helps up to the point where your provider starts rate-limiting.

One further caveat on `verify`: ETags are only MD5 sums for objects that were uploaded in a single part. Anything written to the bucket by another tool using multipart upload will have a composite ETag that cannot be compared, and `tug` reports those as unverifiable rather than as mismatches.

# tug

`tug` pushes a local directory to an S3-compatible bucket. It is deliberately one-way: files move from your machine to the remote, and nothing on the remote ever comes back down or gets removed. If you want a general-purpose two-way sync tool, this is not it. If you want to shove a build output, a static site, or a backup directory at a bucket and have it finish quickly the second time, that is what `tug` is for.

Files are skipped when the local size and modification time match the remote object's, which makes repeat pushes cheap without hashing anything. When you need a stronger guarantee than mtime can give, `tug verify` compares checksums instead.


# ADR: Postgres SKIP LOCKED for background job queueing

**Status:** Accepted. Implemented in Q3.

## Context

Background work currently runs through a job runner we wrote ourselves. We are replacing it with a real queue, and the choice of queue determines what we operate, what we have to build, and what the failure modes look like when a job goes wrong at 3am.

Three properties of our situation shaped the decision. The first is volume: we process roughly 30,000 jobs a day, with observed peaks around 40 per second. Averaged out that is well under one job per second, so the peak is about two orders of magnitude above the mean and still an order of magnitude below what a single Postgres instance handles comfortably as a queue. The second is transactionality: most of our jobs are enqueued as a consequence of a database write, and the job must not become visible to a worker unless that write commits, nor be lost if it does. Any broker that lives outside Postgres gives us this only through a transactional outbox, which means we would be building and operating a Postgres-backed queue anyway, as a staging area in front of the real one. The third is the team: nobody here has run Celery in production, and the operational knowledge required to debug it under load is knowledge we would be acquiring during incidents rather than before them.

We evaluated Celery with Redis, RQ, and queueing directly in Postgres using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.

## Decision

We will queue jobs in a Postgres table and dequeue with `SKIP LOCKED`. Workers claim rows inside the same database they already talk to, and enqueueing happens in the same transaction as the writes that cause it.

Celery with Redis was rejected on operational cost. It is the most capable option of the three and the one that scales furthest, but adopting it means adding Redis to the on-call surface: another datastore to monitor, another persistence and failover story to understand, another set of behaviours to learn under pressure. Set against a peak of 40 jobs per second, that capability buys us headroom we have no plausible path to needing, at a cost we pay every week. RQ is meaningfully simpler than Celery and would have been a reasonable choice, but it still requires Redis, so it carries the operational cost without removing the atomicity problem. Neither broker can commit a job atomically with the database write that produced it, and once an outbox table enters the design, the argument for the broker in front of it becomes an argument about throughput we do not have.

## Consequences

We accept a throughput ceiling in the low hundreds of jobs per second. Beyond that, contention on the queue table and the write amplification of claiming rows stop being negligible, and the design stops being appropriate. Our peak sits comfortably below this, but the ceiling is real and we should treat sustained load approaching it as a signal to revisit rather than to tune.

We accept that we write our own retry and scheduling logic, estimated at around 400 lines: backoff, attempt counts, dead-lettering, and delayed execution. This is code we own and must test, and it is the part of the decision most likely to be underestimated, since the hard cases are the ones that only appear under partial failure. In exchange it is code we can read, which is not true of the equivalent behaviour inside Celery.

We accept that a running job holds a connection from the pool for its duration, which couples worker concurrency to connection limits and makes long-running jobs disproportionately expensive. We will give workers a separate pool from the request path so that a slow job cannot starve web traffic, and we should treat any job whose runtime is measured in minutes as a candidate for decomposition.

The benefits follow from the same design. There is no second datastore in the deployment, no broker to fail independently of the database, and no window in which a job exists in one system but not the other. Enqueueing is an insert, so it participates in transactions, rolls back with them, and is visible to the same tooling and backups as the rest of our data. Inspecting the queue is a `SELECT`.

## Revisiting

Reopen this decision if sustained throughput approaches a few hundred jobs per second, if connection pressure from long-running jobs starts affecting the request path after pool separation, or if our retry and scheduling code grows past the point where maintaining it costs more than learning Celery would have.

It has no retry policy worth the name, no scheduling, and a race under concurrent workers that we have papered over with an advisory lock that serialises all dequeues. It needs to be replaced rather than extended.

Our workload is modest and well understood. We process roughly 30,000 jobs a day, with observed peaks around 40 per second, and we have no roadmap item that would change that by an order of magnitude. The jobs themselves are ordinary application work: sending mail, regenerating derived records, calling third-party APIs on a delay.

The constraint that shaped the decision most is transactionality. Nearly every job we enqueue is enqueued as part of a database write, and the job is meaningless or actively harmful if it runs against a transaction that later rolled back. We have already been bitten by the inverse case, where a commit succeeded and the enqueue was lost. Any broker that lives outside Postgres gives us this guarantee only if we build a transactional outbox in front of it, which means we would be running a Postgres-backed queue anyway, plus a relay process, plus the broker.

Operationally we are a small team with an on-call rotation that we would like to keep boring. We already run Postgres, we already have backups, failover, and monitoring for it, and the people on call already know how to debug it. Adding Redis means adding a second stateful system to that surface, including its persistence and eviction semantics, which are a common source of surprise for teams who have not tuned them before. No one on the team has run Celery in production.

## Decision

We will use Postgres as the job queue, dequeuing with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` against a jobs table. Workers claim a batch of rows inside a transaction, run the work, and delete or reschedule the row on completion. Enqueueing is a plain `INSERT` in the caller's transaction, which gives us atomicity with the surrounding database writes for free and removes the need for an outbox.

## Alternatives considered

Celery with Redis is the default choice in our ecosystem and would have given us retries, scheduling, chords, and a large body of documentation without us writing any of it. We rejected it on two grounds. It requires Redis in the on-call surface for a workload that does not need Redis-level throughput, and it cannot enqueue atomically with a database commit, so we would owe ourselves an outbox regardless. The absence of Celery experience on the team compounds both: Celery's failure modes are well documented but not obvious, and we would be learning them during incidents.

RQ is a lighter answer to the same question and would have cost us less conceptual overhead than Celery. It carries the same two problems, since it is still Redis and still outside the transaction, without Celery's compensating maturity in scheduling and workflow features. Choosing it would mean accepting the operational cost of a broker while getting less back for it.

## Consequences

We accept a throughput ceiling. A Postgres-backed queue of this design runs comfortably into the low hundreds of jobs per second and then degrades, primarily through lock contention and table bloat from the delete churn. At 40 per second peak we have an order of magnitude of headroom, but this is the constraint that will eventually force a revisit.

We accept that we own the parts Celery would have given us. Retry with backoff, dead-lettering, delayed and periodic scheduling, and worker heartbeat and recovery come to roughly 400 lines of application code that we now maintain and test. The scope is bounded and the semantics are ours to define, which is worth something, but it is code that would otherwise not exist.

We accept that a running job holds a database connection for its duration, because the claim transaction stays open while the work executes. Long jobs therefore consume pool capacity that web traffic would otherwise use. We mitigate this by giving workers a separate connection pool with its own limit, so a burst of slow jobs cannot starve request handling, and by keeping a hard timeout on job execution.

Two operational obligations follow from the design. The jobs table needs autovacuum tuned more aggressively than our defaults, since high-churn queue tables bloat quickly and the dequeue query is sensitive to it. Queue depth and oldest-job age need to be on the same dashboard and alert path as our other Postgres metrics.

We should revisit this decision if sustained throughput approaches 200 jobs per second, if queue contention shows up in Postgres wait events during normal operation, or if we acquire a requirement for fan-out or workflow orchestration that our own scheduling code cannot reasonably express.

If sustained volume approaches that ceiling we will need to revisit this decision rather than tune our way past it, and the natural successor is a dedicated broker with an outbox, which is the design we deferred here rather than rejected outright.

We take on code we would otherwise have inherited. # ADR-014: Use Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` for background job queueing

## Status

Accepted. Implemented in Q3 2026.

## Context

Background work currently runs on a job runner we wrote ourselves: a table of pending work, a polling loop, and advisory locking bolted on after the first duplicate-execution incident. It has no scheduling, no retry policy worth the name, and no visibility beyond a log line per attempt. Every team that needs deferred work has learned its quirks by breaking it. We want to replace it before it acquires more callers.

Our workload is modest and unlikely to change shape soon. We process roughly 30,000 jobs a day, with observed peaks around 40 per second during the morning import window. The jobs are mostly short: outbound email, thumbnail generation, third-party sync calls. A handful run for minutes rather than seconds.

The requirement that drove the decision is transactional enqueue. Most of our jobs exist because a database write happened, and they are wrong if that write rolls back. A user invitation that is emailed but not recorded, or a sync job for a row that never committed, produces support tickets we have already seen under the current runner. Any broker that lives outside Postgres cannot give us this directly. The standard remedy is a transactional outbox, where the job is written to a Postgres table inside the business transaction and a relay process forwards it to the broker. That works, but it means we operate the broker *and* the outbox, and the outbox is itself a Postgres queue, which is the thing we were trying to avoid writing.

We also weighed operational cost. We run Postgres today with backups, failover, and an on-call rotation that understands it. Redis would be a second stateful system on that rotation, with its own durability configuration, memory-pressure failure modes, and upgrade path. Finally, nobody on the team has run Celery in production. Its configuration surface is large, and its failure modes are learned rather than deduced.

## Decision

We will implement job queueing on Postgres, using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to hand rows to workers without contention. Jobs are rows in a `jobs` table. Producers insert them inside the same transaction as the writes that motivate them, so enqueue is atomic by construction and no outbox is required. Workers poll in a short transaction, claim a batch with `SKIP LOCKED`, and mark terminal state on completion.

We will write the surrounding machinery ourselves: exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, a dead-letter state, `run_after` for delayed and scheduled work, and a reaper for jobs whose worker died mid-execution. We estimate this at about 400 lines, and we accept it as code we own and must test.

## Alternatives considered

Celery with Redis was the default expectation and the strongest candidate on features: mature retry semantics, scheduled tasks, chords and chains, and an ecosystem of monitoring tools. We rejected it on the combination of a new on-call system, no team experience, and the outbox we would still have to build to get transactional enqueue. Its scaling headroom is real but irrelevant at 40 jobs per second.

RQ is simpler than Celery and would have been quicker to adopt, but it shares the Redis dependency and the enqueue-atomicity gap while giving up Celery's maturity in exchange. It removed the argument for Celery without removing the reason we did not want either.

## Consequences

The ceiling on this design is a few hundred jobs per second, set by transaction throughput and polling overhead rather than by anything we can tune away. We have roughly an order of magnitude of headroom over current peak, which we judge sufficient for the next few years but not indefinitely.

Retry and scheduling logic is now our code, so its bugs are our bugs and its semantics are undocumented until we document them. We will cover the claim, retry, and reaper paths with tests before the first migration, and treat the module as owned by the platform team rather than shared.

Long-running jobs hold a pooled connection for their duration. At current volumes this is affordable, but it couples job duration to connection-pool sizing in a way that will not be obvious to the next person who writes a ten-minute job. Workers will run on a pool separate from web traffic so that a slow job degrades background work rather than user requests, and we will alert on jobs exceeding a duration threshold.

Queue depth, oldest-pending-job age, and dead-letter count become ordinary Postgres queries, which means our existing dashboards and ad-hoc SQL work on job state without new tooling. That is a genuine gain over an opaque broker, and it partly offsets the monitoring ecosystem we gave up with Celery.

We will revisit this decision if sustained throughput passes 200 jobs per second, if job execution begins to affect primary database latency, or if we find ourselves reimplementing workflow features such as chaining or fan-out joins. Reaching any of those points should trigger a new ADR rather than incremental extension of the queue we are building here.

# ADR-0014: Use Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` for background job queueing

**Status:** Accepted. Implemented in Q3.

## Context

Background work is currently handled by a job runner we wrote ourselves: a table of pending work, a polling loop, and an advisory-lock scheme to keep two workers from picking up the same row. It has held up, but it has no retry policy worth the name, no scheduled or delayed execution, and no visibility into why a job failed. Rather than continue extending it, we evaluated moving to something with an established operational story.

Three requirements shaped the evaluation. First, jobs must become visible to workers only if the transaction that enqueued them commits, and must always become visible if it does. A user signs up, we write the user row and enqueue a welcome email, and neither half may survive without the other. Second, our volume is modest and expected to stay that way: roughly 30,000 jobs a day, with bursts to about 40 per second. Third, we have a small on-call rotation that currently pages on Postgres and the application tier, and nobody on the team has run Celery in production.

## Decision

We will use Postgres as the queue, with workers claiming jobs via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` against a jobs table in the primary database.

The atomicity requirement is the argument that decided it. A separate broker cannot participate in our database transaction, so getting the same guarantee from Redis would mean writing an outbox: a table of pending publishes, a relay process draining it into Redis, and the deduplication that at-least-once relay delivery forces on every consumer. That is a queue implementation on top of Postgres plus a second queue, which is strictly more machinery than the queue on top of Postgres alone. With `SKIP LOCKED`, the enqueue is an `INSERT` in the same transaction as the writes it accompanies, and the guarantee is free.

The volume figures make the tradeoff easy. Postgres queueing runs out somewhere in the low hundreds of jobs per second, which leaves close to an order of magnitude of headroom above our peak, and our peak is bursty rather than sustained. Adding Redis would put a second stateful system on the on-call surface, with its own persistence configuration, failover behaviour and memory limits, to buy throughput we have no use for.

## Alternatives considered

**Celery with Redis** is the default choice in our language ecosystem and has the richest feature set: retries, scheduling, chains and chords, and a mature worker model. It loses on the two axes we care about. It requires the outbox described above to give us transactional enqueue, and no one on the team has operated it, so the failure modes that make Celery notorious (lost tasks on broker restart, workers wedged on prefetch, the visibility timeout interacting badly with long jobs) would all be learned during incidents.

**RQ** is considerably simpler than Celery and would have been a smaller thing to learn, but it still requires Redis and therefore still requires the outbox. Having paid that cost, we would have less than Celery offers.

## Consequences

We accept a throughput ceiling of a few hundred jobs per second. Beyond that, the polling and row-locking load begins to compete with application queries on the same instance, and the answer would be to move the jobs table to a separate Postgres instance or to migrate to a real broker. We should treat sustained throughput above 200 per second as the trigger to revisit this record rather than waiting for contention to show up as latency on user-facing queries.

We take on roughly 400 lines of retry, backoff and scheduling logic that Celery would have provided. This is the part of the decision most likely to be regretted: the code is easy to write and easy to get subtly wrong, particularly around retry storms after a downstream outage and around jobs that fail between claim and completion. It needs tests that exercise worker death mid-job, and it needs a dead-letter path from the outset rather than added after the first incident.

Long-running jobs hold a pooled connection for their duration, since the claiming transaction stays open while the job runs. This couples job duration to pool capacity in a way that a broker would not, and it means a handful of slow jobs can starve the pool that serves web requests. We are mitigating it by giving workers a separate pool from the web tier and setting a hard job timeout, but the constraint is real and argues for keeping jobs short.

In exchange we add nothing to the on-call surface, we get exactly-once enqueue semantics without a relay, and inspecting the queue is a `SELECT` that anyone on the team already knows how to write.

# Incident postmortem: image upload failures, 2025-07-14

## Summary

Between 09:12 and 11:48 UTC on 14 July 2025, image uploads failed for every user of the platform. The failure began two minutes after the deploy of `media-service` v4.7.0, which introduced a dependency on an `ImageMagick` binary that was absent from the production container image. Roughly 18,000 uploads failed over the 2 hours and 36 minutes the incident was open. No data was lost: uploads either failed outright or were retried successfully once the service recovered, and the retry backlog drained by 11:48.

The most costly part of this incident was not the bug but the 51 minutes between the failure starting and anyone knowing about it. The service returned HTTP 200 with an error body, so the alert on 5xx rate stayed silent, and the first signal we received was a customer support ticket at 09:41.

## Timeline (UTC)

- **09:12** — `media-service` v4.7.0 deployed to production.
- **09:14** — Upload error rate rises from a baseline of 0.2% to 100%. No alert fires; the failing responses carry a 200 status with an error body, and the alert is defined on 5xx rate.
- **09:41** — First customer support ticket arrives.
- **10:03** — An engineer notices the rising ticket volume and begins investigating.
- **10:20** — Cause identified: v4.7.0 changed the thumbnail generator to shell out to `ImageMagick`, which is not installed in the production container image.
- **10:31** — Rollback to the previous version begins.
- **10:44** — Rollback complete; uploads recover immediately.
- **11:48** — Backlog of retried uploads finishes draining. Incident closed.

## What happened

Version 4.7.0 of `media-service` reworked thumbnail generation to invoke the `ImageMagick` binary as a subprocess. That binary is present in the image CI builds and runs tests against, but not in the image we ship to production, because the two images are built from different Dockerfiles that have drifted apart. Every upload reaching the thumbnail step therefore failed at the point of invoking a binary that did not exist, and since the upload handler treated thumbnail failure as a recoverable application-level error rather than a server error, it returned a 200 response carrying an error payload. Clients read that payload correctly and reported the upload as failed to users, but every layer of our monitoring between the client and the service saw a successful request.

## Contributing factors

Three independent gaps had to line up for a missing binary to become a two-and-a-half-hour outage, and each of them is worth treating separately.

The production container image is built from a different Dockerfile than the one used in CI. This means CI cannot, in principle, tell us whether a new runtime dependency will be present in production; the two images are related only by convention and by whoever remembers to update both.

The integration test suite mocks the thumbnail generator. Even had the Dockerfiles been unified, the tests exercising the upload path never invoke the real generator, so the missing binary would not have surfaced. The mock was introduced to keep the suite fast, which is a reasonable goal, but it removed the last place where a dependency error could have been caught before deploy.

The alert measured HTTP status rather than application-level success. Our alerting assumed that a failing request produces a failing status code, and the upload handler's error semantics violated that assumption without anyone noticing the mismatch. This is the factor that converted a bad deploy, which should have been a five-minute rollback, into an outage measured in hours.

## Action items

1. **Unify the CI and production container images.** Build one image from one Dockerfile and promote the artefact CI tested through to production, rather than rebuilding at deploy time. (Owner: Platform)
2. **Run at least one integration test against the real thumbnail generator.** The suite can keep its mocks for breadth, but the primary upload path needs an unmocked test that would fail if the binary or its dependencies were missing. (Owner: Media)
3. **Alert on application-level upload success rate, not HTTP status.** Add an alert on the ratio of successful uploads to attempted uploads, with a page threshold well below the 100% failure we saw here. (Owner: Media / Observability)
4. **Audit other handlers that return 200 on failure.** Where an error is genuinely recoverable the status may be defensible, but each case needs a corresponding application-level metric, and we should know how many such cases exist. (Owner: Media)
5. **Review the escalation path from support tickets.** Twenty-two minutes passed between the first ticket and an engineer engaging with it; a volume-based trigger from the support queue into on-call would have shortened this. (Owner: Support / On-call)

# Incident postmortem: total image upload failure

**Date:** 2025-07-14, 09:12–11:48 UTC (2h36m)
**Impact:** Image uploads failed for all users. Roughly 18,000 uploads failed. No data was lost.

## Summary

A routine deploy of `media-service` v4.7.0 introduced a dependency on the `ImageMagick` binary, which is not present in the production container image. Every upload that reached the thumbnail generation step failed. The service returned HTTP 200 with an error body, so the alert on 5xx rate never fired, and the failure was invisible to monitoring for 49 minutes until the first customer support ticket arrived. Detection ultimately depended on a person noticing an unusual volume of tickets. Once an engineer began investigating, diagnosis took 17 minutes and the rollback restored service 24 minutes after that. The remaining hour was spent draining the backlog of client-side retries.

## Timeline

- **09:12** — `media-service` v4.7.0 deploys to production.
- **09:14** — Upload error rate rises from 0.2% to 100%. No alert fires; the alert measures 5xx responses and the service is returning 200 with an error body.
- **09:41** — First customer support ticket.
- **10:03** — An engineer notices the ticket volume and begins investigating.
- **10:20** — Cause identified: v4.7.0 changed the thumbnail generator to shell out to `ImageMagick`, which is absent from the production container image.
- **10:31** — Rollback to v4.6.x begins.
- **10:44** — Rollback complete; uploads recover.
- **11:48** — Backlog of retried uploads drains. Incident closed.

## Root cause

The v4.7.0 thumbnail generator invokes an `ImageMagick` binary at runtime. That binary exists in the image CI builds and tests against, but production containers are built from a separate Dockerfile that was never updated to include it. The divergence meant the change passed every gate that ran before deploy and failed on the first request it served in production.

## Contributing factors

Three independent gaps had to line up for this to become a two-hour outage, and each one is worth treating separately.

The production container image is built from a different Dockerfile than the one used in CI. This is the proximate reason the missing dependency was not caught: CI validated an artifact that is not the artifact we ship, so a passing build carried no information about whether production would work.

The integration test suite mocks the thumbnail generator. Even had CI used the production image, the tests would not have exercised the code path that shells out to the binary. The mock was presumably introduced to keep tests fast and hermetic, but it removed coverage from exactly the boundary where this class of failure occurs.

The alert measured HTTP status rather than application-level success. The service reported failures as 200 responses carrying an error body, a pattern that is common enough in our API surface that the monitoring gap likely extends well beyond uploads. This factor is the one that turned a bad deploy into a long incident: the technical fault lasted 90 minutes, but roughly 50 of those minutes were spent with nobody aware anything was wrong.

## What we are changing

The most valuable fix is the alerting one, because it shortens every future incident of this shape regardless of cause. We will alert on application-level upload success rate rather than status code, with a threshold sensitive enough to fire within a few minutes of a 100% failure, and audit other services for endpoints that report failure inside a 200.

Second, the two Dockerfiles need to be reduced to one, with CI building the same image that is promoted to production. If a single Dockerfile is not achievable quickly, an interim check that diffs the installed package sets between the two images and fails the build on divergence would have caught this specific change.

Third, the integration suite should exercise thumbnail generation against the real binary in the real image, at least in one end-to-end test. A single unmocked upload test running against the production artifact would have failed this deploy in CI.

Finally, this deploy served 100% failures for 90 minutes with no automated signal. A post-deploy smoke test that uploads an image and verifies the resulting thumbnail, gating promotion or triggering automatic rollback, would have bounded the impact to a few minutes independent of whether anyone was watching a dashboard.

## What went well

Once investigation began, diagnosis was fast: 17 minutes from first look to identified cause on a failure mode with no useful alerting and a misleading status code. The rollback path worked as intended and restored service in 13 minutes. Client retries meant no uploads were permanently lost, though they also produced the backlog that extended the incident by an hour after service recovered.

## Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 09:12 | `media-service` v4.7.0 deployed to production |
| 09:14 | Upload error rate rises from 0.2% to 100%; no alert fires |
| 09:41 | First customer support ticket opened |
| 10:03 | Engineer notices ticket volume and begins investigating |

| 10:44 | Rollback complete; uploads recover |

The thumbnail generator in v4.7.0 was rewritten to shell out to `ImageMagick`. That binary is present in the development and CI environments but absent from the production container image, so every thumbnail generation attempt failed at the point of process invocation. The upload handler caught the failure and returned it to the client as an error body carried inside an HTTP 200 response, which is the existing convention in that service for application-level errors.

That convention is what suppressed detection. The upload alert was defined against the 5xx rate, and the 5xx rate never moved, because the service was cheerfully returning 200 for every failed upload. From the monitoring system's perspective the service was healthy for the entire duration of a complete outage. Detection therefore fell to customers, who took 29 minutes to file the first ticket, and then to an engineer noticing that tickets were accumulating, which took another 22 minutes. Three things had to be true at once for this to reach production undetected. The production container image is built from a different Dockerfile than the one CI uses, so a dependency added to the CI image is not added to the shipped image and nothing in the build compares them. The integration test suite mocks the thumbnail generator, so the tests that would have exercised the new code path never invoked the binary and passed identically in both environments. And the alerting measured transport-layer status rather than application-level success, so a service that reports its own errors inside a 200 response is by construction unmonitorable by that alert.

Each of these is individually defensible and collectively they removed every layer that could have caught the problem: the build could not catch it, the tests would not catch it, and the alerts could not see it.

The integration suite should exercise the real thumbnail generator against the production image in at least one test, so that a missing runtime dependency surfaces as a test failure rather than a customer ticket.
